review:
Dota 2 is one of the best games ever made — and also one of the hardest to recommend without a warning label. It has a massive, thriving player base with millions of concurrent users, a thriving esports scene, and a level of depth that few games can match. But it is also brutally complex, unforgiving to newcomers, and demanding in a way that can feel overwhelming.

The Good: A Game That Rewards Dedication

The core of Dota 2 is sublime. Every match is a chess game played at real-time speed, where decisions matter, teamwork is essential, and the skill ceiling is essentially infinite. The game is free-to-play with no pay-to-win mechanics, which is remarkable given its scale. The hero pool is enormous — over 100 characters, each with unique abilities, roles, and playstyles — and the item system, map dynamics, and meta shifts keep the game fresh even after thousands of hours. When everything clicks, Dota 2 delivers a sense of satisfaction that few other games can match. The million-plus online count is proof that this formula works.

The Bad: A Mountain of Complexity

Here is the catch: Dota 2 is incredibly hard to learn. The mechanics are deep and layered — last-hitting, denying, creep aggro, stacking, pulling, ward placement, timings, power spikes, and dozens of other systems that are never explained properly in-game. Then there is the hero problem: with 100+ characters, each having multiple abilities, remembering what every single one does is a massive undertaking. You need to know not just your own hero, but every enemy hero's abilities, cooldowns, and counters. That knowledge gap is brutal for new players.

The learning curve is less a curve and more a cliff. The game does have a tutorial, but it barely scratches the surface. Most players learn through trial, error, and a lot of frustration — often while being flamed by teammates. It is not a game you can casually pick up and enjoy immediately. It demands time, patience, and a willingness to lose repeatedly while you figure things out.

Verdict!

Dota 2 is a masterpiece of game design, but it is not for everyone. If you are willing to invest the time to learn its complex mechanics and memorize the abilities of over 100 heroes, you will find one of the deepest and most rewarding competitive games in existence. If you want something you can learn in a weekend, look elsewhere. It is brilliant, it is massive, and it is merciless — and that is exactly why its community loves it!

review:
The current Dota 2 is clearly not the work of Ice Frog, but a typical valve style design

After version 7.0, the designer added new things that disrupted the high degree of freedom team design built by Ice Frog in its early days.

Striving to bind all players together and let one person who makes a mistake punish all those who don't, Valve calls it "teamwork", which is really humorous


This design is reflected in Blizzard's Storm Heroes, but it has already been featured in Valve's l4d1 or 2

However, this is a 'low degree of freedom team', and good design should provide players with multiple ways to give back to the team, rather than completing the designer's tasks. There should not be too many constraints between teammates, and tasks that can be completed by one person should not be forcibly assigned to two people. Let the strong lead the game to victory, rather than letting the weak drag one by four. Allowing the existence of 3v5 or even 2v5 like Dota1 is closer to a high degree of freedom team. And this is closer to the design concept of ice frogs.

Perhaps they are paired up with some friends that are learning the game and instead of playing the position or role that they should be playing they decide to follow their buddy so they can stick together. I do wish that they had a better queue system similar to that of League of Legends so that when you queue for a match you select a couple of heroes that you want to play as and the role you want to play them as and that's who and where you play. I know that isn't for everyone but it would make games better in my opinion. For the players that are new and want to run around with their buddies talking in Discord and all of that you should definitely play the bot matches. That is what they are for. So you can learn what to do and where to go. 

All in all though the game is great. Will there be a toxic aspect to the game, of course. review:
I’m not really into competitive games, but Dota 2 is something else. All the heroes are cool, the game itself is excellent, and I genuinely have a great time playing positions 4 and 5. Mid is fun too, though. Man, my Skywrath Mage is something special.

One of the things I like most about Dota 2 is how much variety there is in the way you can play. The heroes feel distinct from one another, and even when two of them share some similarities, they can still offer completely different experiences. There are so many abilities, item combinations, and builds to experiment with that you can keep coming back to the same hero and still find new ways to play. Some heroes are flexible enough to fit into multiple positions, too, which makes things even more interesting. A hero's usual role doesn't necessarily have to be the only way to play them, and sometimes the fun comes from trying something that looks completely ridiculous on paper. I mean, come on, let me play Queen of Pain as a position 5. You can flame me all you want; I'm having fun.

The different builds are a big part of that appeal. You're not always locked into one specific way of playing a character, and adapting your items to the match can make a real difference. The facets also added another interesting layer to hero customization, giving you more reasons to experiment with different approaches. Whether they're still available in their original form or have changed over time, that kind of system is exactly what I enjoy about Dota 2: having more than one way to approach a hero instead of simply following the same build every game.

The hero leveling system is another nice touch. It's satisfying to level up your favorite characters, and the progression makes playing them feel even more rewarding. I especially like unlocking new chat wheel lines. There's something funny about having the perfect voice line ready for the right moment, whether you're celebrating a great play, teasing the enemy, or just being an absolute menace in chat. It's a small feature, but it gives you another reason to keep playing and makes your favorite heroes feel a little more personal.

The skins are great, and there's so much customization available for the heroes. Some combinations look fantastic, and putting together an appearance you really like is part of the fun in itself. And that Drow Ranger skin? Goodness gracious... As soon as I have some money to spare, I'm buying it. I might even buy two if I can. She looks so damn cool.

Of course, not everything about Dota 2 is great. The reporting system can be pretty frustrating, especially when it feels like people can spam reports against you and potentially get you penalized. Reports should be useful for dealing with genuinely disruptive behavior, not something players can abuse because they're angry about a match or don't like the way someone plays. There's a difference between deliberately ruining a game and picking an unconventional hero or trying an unusual build. If I'm playing Queen of Pain as a position 5, that might not be what you wanted to see in your match, but it doesn't automatically mean I'm trying to ruin it. Sometimes people just want to play differently, and the game gives them enough flexibility to make that interesting.

The matches themselves are another reason I enjoy the game. There are shorter modes for when you don't have much time to spare, but I think some of the best moments happen when a match goes on for a while. Games can become increasingly chaotic as both teams get stronger, and a match that seems decided can still turn around if someone makes a mistake or a team pulls off an incredible play. Those long games can be exhausting, of course, but there's something satisfying about a hard-fought match where every decision matters. Not every game needs to be a quick victory to be memorable.

There's a lot to learn, too. Between the heroes, abilities, items, matchups, positions, and all the different ways you can approach a game, there's always something new to figure out. Even after you've played for a while, you can still discover a build you hadn't considered or realize that a hero works better in a role you never expected. That depth is part of what makes Dota 2 so appealing to me. You don't necessarily need to be obsessed with competitive play to enjoy experimenting with the game and finding your own way to have fun.

Anyway, that's pretty much it. Dota 2 has its frustrating moments, and the community can certainly make things worse sometimes, but the sheer amount of variety, customization, and personality packed into the game makes it easy to understand why people keep coming back to it. I may not be the most competitive player around, but I know what I enjoy, and Dota 2 gives me plenty of reasons to keep playing.

Dota 2 is one hell of a game.

review:
When the game is playable, its actually not that bad and quite fun. However as as new dota player in the year 2026 there are several barriers holding you back from ever actually enjoying the game, and none of those barriers are related to the gameplay itself. The real fundamental problem’s I have with this game is the matchmaking and new player mode. 

I understand that having a new player on your team is frustrating, but I just don’t believe that them playing an ‘easier’ champion will at all fix the problem of them being new to the game. Just because someone is playing tidehunter instead of lycan in pos3, doesn’t mean they won’t still just be adjusting to the game. They still won’t understand pulling enemy melee minions to your ranged creep or what the enemy heros do, or about a thousand other macro/micro things to do with dota. I can understand that it may be easier to learn the game on an easier champ, but I think players should have the right to learn on whoever they want to learn on. I realize it’s easier just to hit R on tidehunter but if the player wants to play lycan I think they should be allowed to play lycan. What new player mode actually does is drive new players to not want to play the game since they can’t play the characters they want to play. 

Furthermore, the amount of bot lobbies I have encountered is just disgusting. What’s even worse, is when you get bots on your team but the enemy team gets not bots, leading to an unfair game state. Or when there are bots on each team and it comes to a challenge of which team can farm the bots better to get more gold. I don’t mean bots as a derogatory term by the way, truthfully they are bots created to sell accounts. I have got games before where they send out a message saying the game needs to go a certain length and to let them get some amount of kills for it to be counted so their accounts can be sold later on. 

It is very frustrating to attempt to play the game and you are just placed in bot lobby after bot lobby, this limbo where no matter how much you play you are eternally stuck not playing or really learning the game. Stomping bots is not how you learn the game, nor is it enjoyable in the slightest. I have never left a game or done anything to place myself into low prio q and my reputation score has only gone up since I started playing. However, I am still stuck in lobbies where I have bots on either my team the enemy team or both. In fact, with 99.3 hours played in a match, I am still receiving games where I am the only human in the lobby. 

In summary, I believe that when the game is playable, when there are no bots on your team or the enemy team, and you have a team willing to play their position the game is very enjoyable. However you really do have to suffer through at least 100 hours of just bot lobbies, which is disgusting, and also have to get through new player mode, which is just disheartening. I wish I could give a neutral review, since I still feel like despite having 162 hours in the game (this means 62 hours in queue, or 62 hours of uncounted games because yes sometimes bot lobbies aren't counted so you just waste time since leaving will put you in low prio q), just now is it becoming playable, which is unacceptable for how much this game is praised and put on a pedestal. I understand and get games taking a heavy commitment to get into, but I would rather get hard stomped by players better than me for 100 hours than just turn my brain off against bots.

review:
Unfair Punishment System Is Ruining Dota 2

I have spent a significant amount of time and money on Dota 2, but I am extremely disappointed with the current punishment system.

The game repeatedly gives me Low Priority penalties, ranked matchmaking restrictions, and reduces my Behavior Score and Communication Score, even when the situation involves temporary technical issues rather than intentional misconduct.

Sometimes my internet connection drops or my computer freezes. I always try to reconnect within a few minutes, but the system still treats me as if I deliberately abandoned the game.

In one of my recent matches, I was simply taking my time to choose a hero. I was still connected to the game, yet I received another penalty.

My Behavior Score and Communication Score have now dropped to critically low levels, making the overall matchmaking experience increasingly frustrating.

The worst part is that the system creates a vicious cycle: once your scores drop, recovering them becomes extremely difficult.

I regularly purchase in-game items and have financially supported this game because I genuinely enjoy Dota 2. However, spending money on a game that repeatedly punishes you without properly considering the circumstances feels incredibly disappointing.

Valve needs to seriously reconsider how its automated punishment system works. There should be a clear distinction between intentional griefing, abandoning games on purpose, and temporary technical difficulties.

Players deserve transparency, fairness, and the opportunity to appeal questionable penalties.

I cannot recommend Dota 2 in its current state.

Until Valve improves its punishment system and starts taking legitimate player complaints seriously, my review will remain negative.

review:
Dota 2 — A Masterpiece That Can Drive You Insane

Dota 2 is one of the deepest and most rewarding competitive games ever made. After spending a significant amount of time playing it, you start to realize that this is not just a MOBA about destroying the enemy Ancient. It is a game of strategy, psychology, teamwork, mechanics, and decision-making, where even the smallest mistake can cost you the entire match.

✅ What Makes Dota 2 Great

Insane strategic depth. The combination of hero drafts, item builds, counters, map control, vision, rotations, and team fights makes every match unique. There is always something new to learn, regardless of your experience.

Incredible hero diversity. The roster offers an enormous variety of playstyles. Every hero has its own strengths, weaknesses, and potential, and the right combination of abilities can completely change the outcome of a game.

High skill ceiling. Dota 2 rewards game knowledge, mechanical skill, positioning, timing, and smart decision-making. Winning through experience and understanding the game feels genuinely satisfying.

Unforgettable comebacks. Few things compare to turning around a seemingly impossible game with one perfectly executed team fight or by punishing a critical enemy mistake.

Regular updates and evolving strategies. Balance patches and gameplay changes keep the experience fresh and force players to adapt instead of relying on the same strategies forever.

Free-to-play done right. All heroes are available without grinding to unlock them or purchasing them individually. The competitive gameplay remains accessible to everyone.

❌ The Problems

Toxicity. Flaming, blaming, griefing, and teammates giving up prematurely can ruin even the best matches. Sometimes the hardest part of Dota 2 is not defeating the enemy team but maintaining your composure.

Inconsistent matchmaking. Some games feel balanced and competitive, while others seem decided by the difference in team coordination long before the final fight.

A brutal learning curve. New players face an overwhelming amount of information, from hundreds of abilities and item interactions to advanced macro decisions. Dota 2 demands patience and dedication.

Frustrating team dependency. Individual skill matters, but this is still a team game. You can make the right decisions and play your role well without being able to compensate for every mistake made by four other players.

Long matches and mental fatigue. A single game can demand a serious investment of time and concentration. Losing after a long, hard-fought match can be exhausting, especially in ranked.

Balance and meta issues. Some patches make certain heroes or strategies feel disproportionately strong. Adapting is part of the experience, but not every meta is equally enjoyable.

⚡Final Thoughts

Dota 2 is a game that can be incredibly frustrating and unbelievably satisfying, sometimes within the same match. It tests your patience, punishes your mistakes, rewards your knowledge, and constantly reminds you that there is always room for improvement.

Despite its flaws, the depth of its gameplay is exceptional. The satisfaction of mastering a difficult hero, outsmarting your opponents, coordinating a perfect team fight, or winning a match that seemed completely lost is what keeps the game compelling in the long run.

It is definitely not a game for everyone. If you want something casual, relaxing, and consistently fair, Dota 2 might test your patience. But if you enjoy competitive challenges, strategic freedom, and a game with an incredibly high skill ceiling, there is hardly anything quite like it.

Dota 2 is not perfect, and sometimes it makes you question your sanity. But when everything clicks, it reminds you why you keep coming back.

Final rating: 9/10.

A legendary competitive game with unmatched strategic depth, endless replayability, and a community that can be both its greatest strength and its biggest weakness.

GG WP. See you on the battlefield.

The game crashes, and then it takes 10 full minutes to verify files on an SSD?! Boom, loss of reputation. The game fails to launch a match?! Boom, loss of reputation. The worst part is that your reputation drops for any reason at all: if the opponents didn't like losing to you, they'll just spam you with dislikes and reports. If your teammates don't like how you play, they'll spam you with dislikes and reports. People are terrified of typing in chat or using voice comms because they know they'll get reported instantly. Players who have never insulted anyone in their lives can't speak or type—not even because of other players, but simply because their game crashed or their internet dropped. And the funniest thing is that you can lose 400 reputation points just by crashing without any option to reconnect, yet earning those 400 points back will take you anywhere from 50 to 100 matches, because in every game there will always be someone commending you and someone disliking you. On top of that, matchmaking randomness has obviously gotten even worse than before. How else do you explain getting the exact same teammate 10 times in a row, who doesn't even know how to play at all? I strongly advise against wasting your time on this. review:
This game is BUGGY. UI elements can get stuck on screen (try holding shift and queueing up some move actions while you're dead, you'll have shit stuck on your screen the rest of the game). And the tutorials are totally broken, sometimes locking your hero to be centered on your screen and disabling screen panning which was so distressing being forced to use that in an RTS engine like this that I almost uninstalled the game until I figured out it was a tutorial only thing.

The bots are beyond stupid, even the bots labelled "unfair" I can go 22-1 against playing Viper, they don't listen to your pings even though they're constantly pinging and announcing what they're doing, and the last match I played against the bots my team all went to Roshan, attacked him, got him to 5% hp, then all... walked away for no reason leaving me to try and kill the last of Roshan's hp or just leave it there to be sniped by the opposing teem. That's such a catastrophically stupid move I don't even know where to begin. Not only that, the bots after the 25 minute mark like to just all group up and walk back and forth over the same tiny patch of map the rest of the game, leaving you to do everything yourself. I often find myself frantically pinging barracks as I get the AI to help me push a lane, we take down the final tower on the lane, then instead of killing the barracks the bots just..... leave to go glitch around in the jungle? They also won't stay in their lanes during the laning phase and seem to have absolutely no idea what role they're supposed to fill with their characters or what lane they're supposed to go to, so when I play a carry I have to just outplay the shit out of the enemy bots or else I'm just going to die over and over since nobody comes to safe lane to help me. I know there's like 128 characters or whatever and having bots play them all correctly is hard, but Valve isn't a small indie game company and they have to reap what they sow. You can't just put bots and tutorials in the game and then leave them completely broken and beyond stupid forever. (Or, I guess you can?)

The few times I tried the new player mode recently it just queued me up against Medium bots and no human players, when I was already stomping the Unfair bots. Maybe nobody plays this game in US West anymore but jeez I really didn't want to play a bot match where I don't know for certain it's a bot match until I see all my teammates walking back and forth between two trees in the jungle 25 minutes into the match. This is when I realized that teamwork is like 95% of this game and while you can go try and solo the map, the game is designed for moves on towers, bases, or even pushing lanes quickly to all be group tasks, and when the AI just checks out entirely you feel more lonely and depressed than if you were in an empty lobby just playing against the creeps alone.

If I had the internet connection, I would be willing to play online, but this game you really need to have like... a stack, I think it's called? Like friends, to play it with you. People that will strategize with you, talk to you about what they're doing, learn from mistakes, make plays. I'm weak and old now and I really don't want to argue with people over the internet I've never seen before and will never see afterwards, so I don't feel comfortable aiming for this level of strategy with randos. I would like to have friends play this with me, but it's so intimidating to them I can't even finish a single bot stomp match with my close friends before they want to disconnect and play something else.

I think that this game is good. I would recommend this game if you are in a collegiate esports team or have a lot of friends that are still willing to play MOBAs together with you. Competitively, it's fine as far as I am aware. But as a solo player, it's just terrifying. It's like staring into the abyss. You can fool yourself into having fun with the bots for awhile, but you'll quickly outgrow them and just stagnate if you don't have the means (friends, internet, time...) to continue.

review:
"Carried more animals than Noah" is a popular gaming slang phrase and insult used in multiplayer team games like Dota 2, League of Legends, and Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO).
What It Means
• The "Carry" Role: In tactical and multiplayer online games, a "carry" is a player who becomes powerful late in the match and is expected to lead or win the game for the team.
• "Animals": A slang term used by gamers to describe teammates who play poorly, make bad decisions, or act wild and uncoordinated.
• The Joke: To say someone "carried more animals than Noah" means a player had to single-handedly drag a terrible, underperforming team to a victory—mockingly comparing their effort to Noah carrying pairs of every animal on his ark during the biblical flood.

review:
★★★★☆ - - - 7,000 Hours Later, (1k hours from alt account with the same rank) STILL haven't figured it out why am i in this homicide dungeon 

After 7,000 hours, think I'm finally qualified to review Dota 2. this isn't a game anymore. It's a long-term commitment with occasional gameplay. The game itself is still incredible. But the experience surrounding the game is what i would like to point out.

● The Report System
You can get reported for simply because someone didn't like your decision or yourself personally, not the gameplay you've given to the team as contribution. And sometimes losing a game apparently gives people enough motivation to investigate your entire steam profile and somehow involve your family tree.
Bro, I missed one stun. I didn't insult your ancestors.

● Behavior Score
Honestly, i like the concept. It actually gives toxic players consequences, and restricting certain features for extremely low behavior scores makes sense. It's basically dota saying: “𝘠𝘰𝘶'𝘷𝘦 𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘮𝘪𝘤𝘳𝘰𝘱𝘩𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘷𝘪𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘦𝘴. 𝘗𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘧𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵.” 

● The Great MMR Reset
After all the MMR inflation and resets, matchmaking can sometimes feel like opening a loot box. You don't really know what you're getting. You just pray that your four teammates are locked in, awake, and emotionally present.
If someone is already AFK, feeding, or typing “gg” before the horn, you already know where this is going.

And yet, somehow, dota is still dota, -everything can work (cr:BigDaddyn0tail)
There's always something new to learn. someone makes the perfect initiation, another buys back, the carry gets the crucial item, and suddenly a completely lost game becomes the greatest match you've ever played. ONLY THEN, you queue again because apparently 7,000 + 1000 hours wasn't enough suffering.

review:
Dota 2 is one of the deepest competitive games ever made, and it is completely free.

Every one of the 120+ heroes is unlocked from day one. You never pay for power: the only things for sale are cosmetics. Few free-to-play games are this fair.

The depth is unmatched. Every match is different because of the hero picks, item builds, map control, and how your team works together. Even after years, you still learn something new: a better item timing, a smarter rotation, or a hero interaction you never knew about. When your team executes a perfect teamfight, nothing else in gaming feels quite like it.

Valve still supports it. Big patches regularly change the map, heroes, and items, so the meta never feels stale. The Linux version runs natively on Vulkan, which is a nice bonus.

It is not for everyone, though:
- The learning curve is brutal. Expect your first 100 hours to feel like a tutorial. Play bot matches and Turbo mode first.
- Matches take 35-50 minutes, and leaving early gets you penalized.
- The community can be toxic. Mute early and focus on your own game.

If you have the patience to learn it, Dota 2 rewards you like almost no other game. Highly recommended for players who enjoy strategy, teamwork, and constant improvement.

10/10 - would lose my mid lane again.

review:
The game has a very steep learning curve but is easy to pick up. Its complex in the way music is complex. 
During the time of writing this, I would not consider myself a "skilled" or even "alright" player. 

    That being wrote, the experience in learning it is more like a journey. If you are not willing to go for a ride, then the game is not willing to include you.

    If you can be patient in learning (and playing) the game, you will find more than expected when browsing the game store. It's mechanics, teamplay and included items, are all so intricately woven into the game to make it a diverse experience. In most games, there is an obvious choice with an obvious answer. If you come across a powerful build extremely frequently in this game however, you simply came across those who had a similar way of playing the game, like a playstyle. I have seen characters in this game I tried and thought were terrible on the opposing team who constantly defeated me. 

    The gameplay is slow. It takes almost an hour to play a single match. This gives the players a sense of what path they might want to pursue within the game. This means not only are you able to play the same loadout every game, but you it may be better to switch things up depending on your team and your opponents. That is why having patience is so important in this game. You are in it for the long run.

     Despite having patience and being in it for the long run, the game constantly has you on your toes. Dota is very much a strategy game and one move could make or break the game. Now think of that move, but in every minute of the game, that is Dota. It's a 5v5 team game, with a balance of farming, buying, crafting and fighting, with plenty of downtime while also keeping you guessing, "what happens next?" It's complex systems tie well together so well, and each aspect of the game made me desire to explore it in depth. All of this complexity, and yet all to accomplish a single goal: make the enemy base fall.

    Now, like in every online game, all the players might not be enjoyable to play Dota with, but I am reviewing the game itself. I have met pleasant and unpleasant players during my time on Dota, but the points I made still stand.

    So, If you like a game that has pieces of it to learn and constantly improve upon despite their complexity, and how all those pieces come together to form the painting that is Dota, all while planning with a team, planning ahead, and planning your path for your character's power progression, while 
simultaneously improvising your moves and character layout, then this is a game for you.

review:
Too Many Heroes, Too Much to Learn 😂

I wanted to like Dota 2, but the learning curve completely destroyed my patience.

There are so many heroes, abilities, items and strategies that getting started can feel less like playing a game and more like studying for an exam.

I also noticed that newer players often seem to pick the simpler heroes, which honestly makes sense. When you're still trying to understand what's happening, playing a hero with a complicated kit probably isn't helping. 💀

The good thing is that all heroes are free, so the problem isn't unlocking them — it's actually learning what all of them do.

The game clearly has an enormous amount of depth, and I can understand why people spend thousands of hours playing it.

But I didn't have the patience to learn enough of the game to comfortably play against more experienced players.

Dota 2 isn't a bad game — it's just a game that asks for more patience than I have. 😂

If you love competitive games with tons of strategy and don't mind a huge learning curve, you'll probably have a great time.

For me?

review:
Played Dota 2 on and off since Dota 1 on WC3. Recently started playing again after a 6 year break. Many things are new and great but other like the player base remains earily the same. Some of the core issues remained the same because they are untreated. Other aspects are new and gamebreaking. Let it be said that I solely play fun AbilityDraft and Turbo modes.

This game offers something unique compared to other games, a combination of teamwork, high skill, adrenaline, unique situations and unexpected exciting outcomes. That much has all been said before and it's true, albeit with a high learning curve.

The reason why I do not recommend coming back to this game currently is the reporting system in combination with the state of the servers. Because of the declining player base many people flock to playable servers. Communication is key in teamwork but a common language isn't a thing in this game. None of that has ever been enforced. More than half your games will have people that do not speak your language and have a non existing sense of decorum.

People typically fail to see something wrong with their own gameplay and point the finger of blame to others. Valve/Steam has chosen for a community-driven regulation of behaviour and communication. However, with unlimited reports and all reports valid it is impossible to play as a solo player. Often you get reported by a 3-4 man stack. You get reported for people not liking your gameplay, buying the wrong item (in their mind), due to cultural, racist, and other reaasons. Why is this a problem? The lower your score the less you can do, talking, drawing, notifying allies of their ability (CDs). I've seen the list of on the Dota 2 Development Forums regarding this and it's madness. People will still get reported even without the ability to talk.

Not communicating is a flaw. People that fail to communicate their item timings, overarching plans or movement cause problems for their team. It doesn't make sense at all. There are many better alternatives.

Nevertheless and more importantly, Valve/Steam has been aware of this issue since 2025 and continues to steer their course. There was this beautiful quote I read about this game in one of these reviews "I kept agonising that my game was full of idiots until I realised that there were in fact 10." So if you give me the choice as a solo player between playing with randomised people that hate and report me for speaking English, and playing a myriad of other good games, well then I thank you for the opportunity. A team game is only ever as good as the team.

review:
An absolute masterpiece of competitive strategy that offers thousands of hours of unmatched depth—if your sanity can survive it.

Valve’s flagship MOBA stands as the absolute pinnacle of competitive gaming depth. With over 120 unique heroes, hundreds of items, and complex mechanics like creep denying, high-ground vision, buybacks, and dynamic map objectives, no two matches ever play out the same way. The sheer high-dopamine rush of pulling off a game-winning 5-man Black Hole, executing a clutch Aegis steal, or turning around a 60-minute mega-creep comeback provides a high that virtually no other multiplayer title can replicate. It is a game of pure, unadulterated skill where tactical macro-play, item customization, and split-second reaction times matter vastly more than raw mechanical reflexes.

However, that exact depth creates an absurdly intimidating brick wall for newcomers and casuals. The learning curve is not just steep; it is a vertical cliff that takes hundreds of hours of trial and error just to understand basic positioning and lane matchups. To make matters worse, the ranked matchmaking ecosystem can be notoriously toxic, where a single bad play or missed ability can trigger a wave of angry pinging and mic-screaming teammates. Compounding the learning curve is Valve's habit of constantly shifting the goalposts—massive gameplay overhauls routinely rework hero innate abilities, map layouts, and fundamental mechanics, forcing long-time players to constantly relearn the game from scratch.

Yet, despite the rage-inducing losses and complex updates, Dota 2 remains one of the most generous free-to-play packages on Steam. Unlike competing titles in the genre, every single hero is unlocked completely free from the moment you install the game—no grinding or paywalls required. Monolithic lore events, battle passes, and custom arcade maps keep the meta feeling fresh year after year. It is a volatile, high-stakes digital drug that will make you swear off playing forever, only to have you queueing up for "one last match" twenty minutes later.

9/10 — I spent 2,000 hours learning how to properly stack neutral creeps, got flamed in three different languages during a 70-minute loss, and immediately hit 'Find Match' again. The greatest competitive abusive relationship in gaming history.

You can talk about Dota for a very long time. The most important thing you should know:

1. It is precisely thanks to Dota that you will finally be able to find your long-lost father, or find out that your mom liked going to the movies, and in general was in high demand among men.
2. Dota players are great doctors; they can easily diagnose things like: cerebral palsy, autism, Down syndrome, strabismus.
3. If you want to play Dota with a friend, it’s better if you are physically stronger than him, because after a couple dozen matches you’ll want to smash his face.
4.1 If your team won, it’s only thanks to your divine skill.
4.2 If it lost, it’s only because the team was a bunch of idiots; you carried the game as hard as you could.
5. In Dota, the most important thing is to find a scapegoat or an excuse in case of your loss. Be sure to remember how the support stole one last hit from you, or how you were left alone without farm. How the mid laner stood AFK for 15 minutes while the enemies humiliated you. If someone blames you, this will help you bring up a counterargument in your favor. Or better yet, from the very beginning find a scapegoat and start gradually blaming him for bad play. All this will help avoid unnecessary reports. But don’t overdo it: nobody likes strongly toxic players, they get sent to LP first.
6. Don’t try to play Dota for fun; it’s practically impossible. After a certain number of games, even wins won’t make you happy.
7. Always pick Pudge; when you land a hook for the first time, you’ll be incredibly happy.
8. Watch the builds of popular Dota streamers and build heroes exactly like they do, without knowing why or how. When the team asks you, “Why the hell did you buy Basher on Tusk?” you calmly answer, “OMG are you donkeys? That’s how the great streamer HandFromAss229 built him; he knows better than you 2k trash.”

Conclusion: Dota is the best invention of humanity. I’m glad that instead of doing all sorts of nonsense—like studying new sciences and technologies or exploring the boundless expanses of space—I log in and burn in Dota. Thank you very much Valve for the best life in the world.

review:
Please do not play this game!

1. Popularity:

This game is dead; I've just started playing so you can ask how would I know that... basically inferring from lengthy matchmaking times, lag issues with other players, and popularity varies greatly per region.
Plus, what is VALVe's position on bots? If matchmaking can't find enough players for your chosen region(s) in a 'reasonable' timeframe, do they fill with bots?

2. Too many penalties:

In so many instances, you are reprimanded from losing starting Gold, to being forced in other matchmaking categories (like Single Draft) -- like putting a kid in timeout!

3. Hero bans are the oddest thing I've ever seen!

I'm a player where I like a certain character therefore I'll always pick that character; but can't if they're banned often. I think the ban system was put in place for the soul purpose of people potentially buying from the Armory of Heroes they never tried before, but were forced to pick someone else - the Ban system is not for balancing, strictly for some cashflow purposes IMHO.

Furthermore on the bans - I've never played a game where you can ban other characters. Plus, they already give you a metric that estimates your chances against other Heroes, so just let that be your deciding factor; and knowing that if you pick that Hero, it might be at a disadvantage.

Also, it is programmed into the game the popularity of, say Neutrals, when selecting from the Shop. I don't care if 70% of players select a certain Artifact... I'm making my own choice and will not be steered! And that's what it is - we're being steered to quickly choose something; therefore, once you click it, you only add to said popularity.

I have an idea for the Bans though -- copy each matchmaking system (All Pick, Turbo, etc.) and just remove the Hero ban module, then name them like "All Pick (no ban)", "Turbo (no ban)"; very simple & concise.

Conclusion:
I've put a lot of thought into a game I supposedly don't like, but to the contrary, I do believe the concept of the game could flourish if they just make things less a pain in the ass, take out the stupid bans, and stop making everything cost some form of currency!

Yours Truly,

Worst Moba on the market, here is why:

-Last Hit Mechanic : an outdated mechanic that forces you to wait until the enemy minions are extremely low before attacking them so you can get the most important thing in the game, gold. This was extremely frustrating for me since I don't like someone else doing my job for me.

-Shop Confusion: Searching for items in the in game shop requires you to play around 20 hours to learn WHERE and item is then another 5 hours to learn each item individually as to what Attribute they give then another 2 hours per item to learn if you should build them on your hero.

-Broken Champ  Logic : Dota goes on the logic that if all champions are broken then no one really is.. not how it works, this results in a character like Invoker having 5 stuns and slows that he uses on you which renders you unable to play the game 

-Carrier: Cool idea bad implementation. I struggled to use it because the logic behind it is.. crazy. So I have to be close to a "secret shop" for me to buy an item and when I do.. the carrier has to come with the item from the base to me to bring it??? What? I bought it FROM THE SECRET SHOP so give me the fucking item instantly, why is the carrier bringing the item FROM BASE if I wasn't allowed to buy it FROM BASE????

-Bugs: I have less than 10 hours and I already had a pretty annoying bug where the finished item wouldn't be built for some reason.. the result was me selling one of the item components and then buying it again, resulting in a 300 gold loss for me (gold that is hard as fuck to earn because of that dumbass last hit mechanic)

-Queue times: For a game of 500 THOUSAND players having a 7 minute queue time is insane, absolutely crazy. Other games have less than 10k people and it takes you 1-2 minutes to find a match to play. Something is wrong with your server connections.

It's such a shame, the game did really good on some other things, such as:
-allowing you to see if the people in your queue have good karma or good skills (why you would reject the match after a 7 minute queue is beyond me tho)
That's.. it.. there is literally nothing else.

Dota is not "helpful" towards new people in any way, they like their old systems and won't change them for nothing, even if they are extremely badly implemented and flawed beyond touch. 

Dota: 2/10

review:
[h1] Awful Matching System [/h1]

Social Behavior Score: Around 11k (Communication Score is the same)
MMR: 2k Crusader 4
I've been playing online for about 400~500 hours. There are a few states you encounter:

30% -> Idiotic teammates: Even after 1000 matches, people still don't know the basics. I got a Bounty Hunter on my team buying Dagon just for fun, although we needed Spirit Vessel, Khanda, etc and items to stop Bristleback and Necrophos from health regeneration or passive ability. Also, they just refuse to communicate; "Social Behavior Score" doesn't make people nice, it makes people shut up. It just ruins your game. I don't know if they do it on purpose.

20% -> Late Game Feeders: We win early game, laning phase goes perfect, we win team fights THEN one of our pretty teammates decides to just go solo and feed OVER and OVER. Never listens to you. I think they get hypnotized IRL by KOTL or something.

20% -> Perfectly Coordinated Opponent Team: They just beat you up so hard that you can barely breathe. Just can't do anything about that.

5% -> Smurf on Your Team: He just goes 45 0 10 KDA, then your team wins. Extremely boring.

5% -> You Win! But at what cost...: This is most probably a low-MMR thing, but you just played for 80 minutes. They beat you in every aspect. What a miracle that they just got brain-rotted and stupidly lost a team fight without a present buyback. You get an undeserved win. Congratulations.

5% -> I didn't always get "Idiotic teammates" luckily: The opponent plays so badly that you quickly finish the game at 30 minutes. Harsh reality: you sometimes punch the weaker ones in the face.

15% -> A Real Competition: You just deserve it.


After some point, these percentages should change, right? Nah, you can get a 20-loss streak in a row. Of course, this can be different in higher ranks. I am just a newbie trying to enjoy Dota. But getting that frustration over and over exhausts you. Fortunately, they changed the MMR gain, so you get more when you win. However, if I can't enjoy my time in this game, why should I bear it? Losing is not a problem, but losing because someone is trolling your game? That kills the game. You might not be in the mood; I totally empathize with that. Most of the time, I don't play well either; I play so badly sometimes too. But at least I do my best to enjoy the game that 10 people spend time on.

Those are my own opinions. Blah blah. Yeah, that's it

review:
## How to fix Dota 2

* Remove half the jungle camps
* Bring back Unique Attack Modifiers so carries have to choose
* Give more spell-based counterplay while also increasing cooldowns
* Make mana pools something you have to carefully manage again.
* Go back to 6 slots total. No backpack, no scroll slot.
* Rollback the last 8 years of absurd power creep. Only idiots want every patch to be nothing but buffs.
* Remove healing lotuses and wisdom shrines.
* Rework tormentor. If you want it to be a true goal that dictates a team's movements, it should give something more significant than an aghs shard to a random teammate. Give a team a tower they can choose to deploy where one of theirs has died. Make it so the same tower cannot be resurrected more than once.
* Allow players (whose heroes are still alive) to aim tower aggro at enemy heroes, as it is much too easy for experienced players to manipulate tower aggro, while inexperienced players aren't going to have any notion of it. So give the inexperienced players some counterplay.
* Bounty runes are not a bad idea, but they're largely an afterthought. Return them back into the cycle at the main two rune spawn points. There shouldn't be a guarantee of getting a potent combat-oriented rune every time. Make it mean more when someone gets a double damage.
* While we're on the subject, return it to being double damage, and make that double damage extend to spell damage. If PA can get to a point of cleaving a whole team for 4000 damage with a crit without a rune, then high damage ults on heroes like Zeus or Lion should also have the opportunity to put out damage like that if they end up being lucky enough to net the rune that will allow that. It won't break the game, and certainly no more than the currently broken and uninteresting state the game is currently in.
* Add many more trees and make them stay dead longer after a certain point. Leave the tree respawn rate alone during the first 10 minutes, and then make it longer after that. The reason is simple - players should have meaningful counterplay against heroes with a need/usage of trees, but it should be carefully measured so those heroes aren't dumpstered in the laning phase because of this.
* And finally, to add to the tree changes, make more items able to destroy larger amounts of trees. Destructible environments with meaning and purpose to strategic destruction where it matters is more interesting than the tertiary purpose of trees now as mere hindrances for line of sight that have been significantly reduced. Some of the coolest plays in dota are jukes where people used trees and branches to their advantage.

The theme is, of course, COUNTERPLAY. Bludgeoning real counterplay out of the game through arbitrary changes over many years that have caused absurd power creep to just get more and more silly is why the game fails to hold the interest of players for much longer than the time it takes for the new from the last major patch to wear off. Make it mean more to really learn the game again.

Thanks for coming to my TED talk.

review:
Dota 2 is one of the most popular multiplayer games in the world, but popularity does not automatically make a game fun. For many players, Dota 2 can feel less like entertainment and more like a second job that nobody is paying them to do. Between its incredibly complicated mechanics, frustrating matches, and steep learning curve, there are plenty of reasons someone might argue that Dota 2 sucks.

First, Dota 2 is ridiculously complicated. There are dozens of heroes, hundreds of items, and countless abilities to memorize. A new player can spend hours trying to understand what is happening on the screen while experienced players seem to know every possible interaction. Instead of simply learning how to play, beginners have to learn an enormous amount of information before they can even feel competent. A game should be challenging, but Dota 2 sometimes feels like studying for a final exam.

Another problem is how frustrating matches can become. A single mistake can have consequences for the entire team, and one player's bad decision can make the game miserable for everyone else. Even when a player is doing well, the outcome can depend heavily on teammates. This can turn a game that is supposed to be fun into an argument simulator. Losing is already frustrating, but losing after spending nearly an hour in a match can feel especially painful.

The game can also require an enormous amount of time. Matches can last a long time, and players may spend much of that time trying to recover from mistakes or waiting for the other team to make one. Someone who only has a short amount of free time may not want to commit to a game where they could still be playing an hour later. Sometimes you just want to play a quick game, not accidentally dedicate your entire evening to one match.

Finally, Dota 2 can feel like there is always something else to learn. Even after understanding the basics, players have to keep up with new strategies, patches, heroes, items, and changes to the game. This can be exciting for dedicated fans, but for casual players, it can feel exhausting. Instead of relaxing after school or work, you might find yourself wondering why an imaginary wizard just destroyed your entire team.

In conclusion, Dota 2 has plenty of qualities that its fans enjoy, but it also has major drawbacks. Its complexity, frustrating matches, long games, and constant learning requirements can make it feel more stressful than enjoyable. For players who love extremely competitive and complicated games, Dota 2 might be perfect. For everyone else, however, there is always the comforting option of uninstalling it and playing something that does not require a 40-page instruction manual.

review:
"A legendary, endlessly deep masterpiece that will consume your life and test your sanity."

Dota 2 is not just a game; it is an obsession, a lifestyle, and arguably the most complex competitive experience ever created. Stripping away all pay-to-win elements, Valve offers a completely free-to-play arena where every hero is unlocked from the start, making victory entirely dependent on skill, strategy, map awareness, and teamwork.

The learning curve is legendary—a sheer, brutal cliff that takes hundreds of hours just to start climbing properly. But once it hooks you, nothing quite matches the adrenaline rush of a 50-minute comeback, a game-winning teamfight, or executing a flawless combo with your favorite hero. With over a hundred uniquely designed heroes, countless item builds, and constantly evolving metas, no two matches are ever the same.

It is punishing, toxic at times, and will occasionally make you question why you ever press "Find Match." Yet, the sheer depth, strategic brilliance, and unmatched competitive satisfaction keep you coming back for thousands of hours.

If you love high-skill tactical gameplay, deep strategic team dynamics, and games that demand your absolute best, Dota 2 is an unmatched titan.

Pros:

100% free-to-play with zero pay-to-win mechanics (all heroes unlocked)

Astounding tactical depth, complexity, and endless replayability

review:
Dota 2 has slowly lost its identity.

Over the years, the game has become more and more similar to League of Legends, with increasingly overloaded heroes, ridiculous ability upgrades, and mechanics that feel completely out of place compared to what made Dota unique in the first place.

Aghanim’s Shard and Aghanim’s Scepter are a good example. Instead of simply improving or complementing a hero, they can completely change how abilities work and add layers of complexity that often feel absurd rather than interesting.

The same goes for hero passives. Take Lion, who can permanently stack damage through his abilities, or Slark, who can permanently steal enemy Agility. These mechanics may sound interesting on paper, but they contribute to a game where heroes increasingly feel like they have their own mini-games and endless scaling mechanics.

Dota used to stand out because of its unique, unpredictable and strategic gameplay. Now, more and more heroes have overloaded kits, permanent stat stacking, ability upgrades, multiple sources of scaling, and mechanics that make the game feel closer to League of Legends than the Dota I remember.

The problem isn't that the game has changed. Games have to evolve. The problem is that Dota seems to have evolved in a direction that makes it lose what made it Dota.

At this point, I don't feel like I'm playing the same game I originally loved.

review:
Dota 2 is one of the deepest games in terms of how much players need to assess gameplay over an extended amount of time. While other games like FPS’s and fighting games are always played with a time limit, MOBAs will only finish once a base falls.

Dota 2 sports a bigger map with limited teleporting compared to League of Legends so the game has a painstaking process of resource and economy management. From the gold and experience you get from killing creeps, camps, and opponent heroes, you invest in the best items possible.

By the late game, things start to change drastically for both teams. Dota 2 has an obsession with ascension, giving players trillions of ways to go about besting their opponents.

For essential items, teams can purchase Black King Bar, Lotus Orb, and Linken’s Sphere to deter any incoming debuff. There’s also a long list of tier 5 neutral items that players can pick up from creep camps after the 60-minute mark.

Heroes also get stronger and stronger with talent trees that provide amplified stats on either skills or attributes. Players also have the ability to prolong engagements with the Buyback option, which truly matters in the late game where death timers reach minutes.

Looking at the map, you have bounties, runes, and outposts to capture as well as Roshan who provides the Aegis of the Immortal — an item that resurrects a fallen hero to full health and mana — and some cheese.

Needless to say, Dota 2 doesn’t shy away from giving limitless opportunities to players and teams. With no real time limit to the game, you’ll experience thrilling wombo combos and defiant item builds in every match that you play.

Going seven years strong as a casual Dota 2 player, I’m still dumbfounded at a lot of things that I see. It might even take another seven years for me to nail everything down to a tee.

review:
Rating: 8/10 — I hate this game. I also can't stop playing it.

Dota 2 is one of the greatest games ever made.

It is also one of the most mentally exhausting, rage-inducing, time-consuming pieces of shit you can voluntarily install on your computer.

And somehow, both things are true.

The first thing you need to understand about Dota 2 is that this isn't a game you casually play.

You don't "play one game."

You play one game, lose because your mid died three times before minute 10, tell yourself "okay, last game."

Then you queue again.

You lose again.

Now you're angry.

So naturally, you queue for another game because apparently the solution to losing Dota is more Dota.

The Good

When Dota 2 works, it's fucking beautiful.

There is an absurd amount of depth in this game. Hundreds of heroes, ridiculous item combinations, positioning, timings, map control, farming patterns, vision, counter-picks, spell interactions and team coordination.

A single decision can completely change a game.

You can be getting destroyed for 30 minutes and suddenly find one perfect team fight.

One Ravage.

One Chronosphere.

One Black Hole.

One perfectly timed save.

One buyback.

Suddenly the enemy's entire advantage disappears.

That feeling is fucking incredible.

Few multiplayer games can give you that kind of satisfaction.

And the best part?

There isn't always one correct way to win.

You can split push.

You can team fight.

You can rat.

You can snowball.

You can turtle high ground for 40 minutes and somehow turn the game around.

You can completely change your hero's role depending on the situation.

That's what makes Dota special.

The Bad

Now let's talk about the bullshit.

The community.

Holy shit.

Dota players can turn a perfectly normal game into a psychological warfare simulator.

Someone dies once:

"MID DIFF."

Someone misses one spell:

"REPORT SUPPORT."

Your carry doesn't like your item choice:

"NOOB."

Someone disconnects:

"GG."

And somehow, after 15 minutes of everyone flaming each other, the team still has to coordinate a five-man smoke.

It's fucking ridiculous.

And let's not pretend we're innocent.

We've all been that guy.

We've all typed something we immediately regretted.

We've all blamed someone else for a loss.

We've all said:

"If my team wasn't garbage, we would've won."

Would I recommend it?

Yes.

Would I recommend it to my worst enemy?

Absolutely.

Because apparently I don't want them to be happy either.

review:
Found this little indie game while looking for something to play with friends and honestly I'm surprised more people don't know about it.

You pick one of these cute little characters and then you and 9 other players spend some quality time together on a small map. The art is pretty charming and there's a surprising amount of attention to detail for such a tiny studio.

The gameplay is very simple. You just walk around, click on things and occasionally fight some of the local wildlife. There's also a little economy system where you collect gold and buy funny items for your character. Very cozy.

My favorite part is the community. Since this is such a small indie title, everyone seems to know each other. Every match feels like I'm sitting down with a few close friends for a relaxed evening. Sometimes we have disagreements about which direction to walk in, but that's just part of the wholesome co-op experience.

There are also hundreds of characters, which is honestly insane for a game this small. I've been playing for a while and still haven't seen everything. Some of them have really cute names like "Pudge" and "Techies."

The developer is clearly very passionate too. They keep releasing updates and adding new content despite the game being made by what I assume is like three people.

If you have 40 minutes to spare, definitely give this hidden gem a chance.

Would recommend.

review:
Dota 2 is a good game on paper, but it actively punishes experimentation and respects none of your time. The fundamental flaw lies in an automated report system that treats having a bad game as an intentional crime. If you struggle on a core hero like Phantom Assassin or try to test an off-meta build, teammates will immediately weaponize griefing reports against you without any verification. This causes your behavior score to rapidly decay, sending you into lower-tier lobbies(where I obv play)  where report abuse is even more rampant.

Compounding this issue is the total refusal to implement a forfeit option in solo queue. Instead of being able to concede an obvious defeat, players are routinely held hostage in 45 minute slow loss scenarios where the outcome was already sealed at minute twenty. Adding a forfeit option would actually accelerate player skill development exponentially by allowing players to experience and learn from dozens of varied macro scenarios, rather than forcing everyone to sit through unwinnable states where no meaningful skill can be improved.

review:
Dota 2 is one of those games that makes you want to uninstall it, close Steam, and never play again… only to launch 
it again 10 minutes later.

Let’s start with the good.

In terms of gameplay depth, Dota 2 is genuinely one of the most impressive competitive games out there. The huge number of heroes, items, abilities, strategies, combinations, and possible builds makes every match potentially different. There is always something new to learn. Even after hundreds or thousands of hours, you can discover a new mechanic, a new strategy, an unusual build, or realize that you have been playing a hero completely wrong.

And that is exactly why the problems with the game can be so frustrating.

Dota 2 itself is incredibly good.

The problem is everything surrounding that gameplay.

The biggest issue is that one player can completely ruin a match for nine other people.

Someone dies twice in the first few minutes and immediately decides the game is over. Someone starts insulting the entire team. Someone refuses to cooperate. Someone spends 40 minutes farming the jungle while the rest of the team is desperately trying to defend the base. Someone makes one mistake and then spends the rest of the match explaining why everyone else is responsible for losing.

And somehow, the player with 5,000+ hours who is screaming at everyone about how terrible they are will usually make an even bigger mistake five minutes later.

Matchmaking can be another adventure by itself.

Sometimes you get an amazing match where both teams are evenly matched. Every fight matters, every tower matters, and one good decision can completely change the game. You get comebacks, smart rotations, team fights, Roshan contests, clutch saves and genuinely memorable moments.

Those are the games that remind you why Dota 2 is so addictive.

Then you get the opposite.

A completely one-sided match where the outcome is basically decided after 15 minutes, but somehow you still have to spend another 30 minutes watching your Ancient slowly disappear.

At that point you are sitting in front of your monitor thinking:

“Why am I still playing this?”

The match ends.

You click “Play Again.”

And that is probably the most accurate description of Dota 2.

It is a game that can make you angrier than almost anything else, yet somehow convinces you that the next match will be different.

Toxicity deserves its own section.

Dota 2 toxicity has become almost a fundamental part of the experience. Insults, spam pings, sarcastic voice lines, blaming supports for everything, blaming the carry, blaming the mid player, blaming the offlaner, blaming the draft, blaming the matchmaking…

Sometimes it feels like people don't actually queue to win.

They queue to find someone to blame when they lose.

The funniest part is that everyone thinks they are the main character.

Your carry thinks the support is useless.

The support thinks the carry is useless.

The mid player thinks both supports are useless.

The offlaner thinks the mid player ruined the game.

And the enemy team is somehow cheating.

Perfect teamwork.

There is also the problem of smurfs, boosters and unfair matches. Valve has taken measures against smurfing and has banned large numbers of accounts for this kind of behavior, which shows how serious the problem has been. But the fact that these issues have been such a major topic in the community says a lot about how important matchmaking integrity is for a competitive game like Dota 2.

Then there is the learning curve.

Dota 2 is not a game you simply install and understand.

For a new player, it can feel like being thrown into a university exam without ever attending the classes.

There are dozens of heroes to learn, hundreds of items, different roles, abilities, counters, timings, farming patterns, map movements, ward locations, objectives, Roshan timings and countless small mechanics that experienced players take for granted.

A new player can spend hours learning the basics and then meet someone who understands the game far better and gets destroyed in seconds.

The experienced player thinks:

“Easy.”

The new player thinks:

“What the hell just happened?”

But once you finally understand the basics, something changes.

You start seeing the game differently.

You stop simply reacting to things and start predicting them.

You understand why the enemy is moving somewhere. You recognize a potential gank. You know when to fight and when to retreat. You start thinking about item timings, map control, objectives and positioning.

And that is when Dota 2 becomes truly amazing.

Few things feel better than winning a difficult match because your team actually worked together.

A perfectly executed team fight.

A last-second save.

A successful smoke gank.

Stealing Roshan.

Defending your high ground for 20 minutes.

Turning a completely lost game into a comeback.

Those moments are incredible.

And those moments are exactly why people keep coming back.

Dota 2 is not a bad game.

Actually, the opposite is true.

It is an incredibly good game surrounded by an incredible amount of frustration.

Gameplay: 10/10.

Depth: 10/10.

Variety: 10/10.

Teamwork: 10/10 — when your team actually works together.

Learning curve: Pain.

Matchmaking: Sometimes a lottery.

Toxicity: Basically its own game mode.

Amount of time you can lose: Unlimited.

Dota 2 is one of those games where you completely understand why people love it while also completely understanding why they hate it.

You can have the best match of your life and immediately follow it with the worst match imaginable.

You can spend an hour playing perfectly, lose because of one stupid decision, stare at the defeat screen for a few seconds and say:

“That's it. I'm done with Dota.”

Then five minutes later:

“Okay, one more.”

And that's the Dota 2 experience.

I recommend it to anyone who enjoys extremely deep competitive games and is willing to spend hundreds of hours learning, losing, improving, getting tilted, recovering, and occasionally experiencing one of the most satisfying victories a multiplayer game can offer.

For everyone else…

Stay away.

Dota 2 has already taken enough of our time.

I came back to Dota 2 after not playing since 2018, and I honestly can't believe how far the game has fallen.

The current report and punishment system is absurd. Players can report you simply because they don't like the way you played, the hero you picked, a decision you made, or because they need someone to blame for losing. In a competitive game, disagreements and mistakes are inevitable, yet the system gives other players far too much influence over whether you are allowed to continue playing.

I'm convinced that even professional Champions League-level players could join regular matchmaking and still get reported by random teammates who think they know better.

After 1,500+ hours, I also see absolutely no reason to spend money on Dota anymore. Why buy expensive skins or support the game financially when a few angry players can report you and you can end up unable to play? You can literally have hundreds of euros worth of cosmetics on an account and still have your evening ruined because some random kids decided they didn't like how you played.

Dota used to be a game I could recommend. In its current state, I can't.

Constant smurfs or account buyers in the game ruin all the fun. review:
Despite my best efforts, I always return to Dota eventually. No other game matches its depth and complexity. Every match is truly unique, and there are hundreds of small factors to consider in every single one of them. Other multiplayer experiences, even other MOBAs, feel shallow by comparison.

The downsides are the learning curve and the community. You will invest hundreds of hours just to finally start having impact in your games, and you will have to deal with the most emotionally unstable "adults" that our planet has to offer. You will learn about other cultures and how much they all hate each other. You will climb the ranks many times just to discover how little you know about this game. Take it from me: my peak is 4.9k MMR, and I know nothing about Dota.

If you're looking for a game that you can start a lifelong journey of learning with, and you can tolerate the above aspects, then look no further. Dota will welcome you, not with open arms, but with burning spears and hundreds of spiderlings.

review:
Dota 2 is arguably the deepest, most complex, and mechanically flawless MOBA ever made.
Every single one of its 120+ heroes is 100% free to play from your very first match, a consumer-friendly model that leaves its competitors in the dust.
The strategic depth, tactical variety, and sheer adrenaline of a hard-fought victory are unmatched in all of gaming.
However, its legendary difficulty and notoriously harsh community make it a digital gauntlet that will test your sanity.

The Good:

1. True Free-to-Play: No locked characters or paywalls; every piece of gameplay-affecting content is entirely free, with monetization strictly limited to cosmetics.
2. Infinite Strategic Depth: With complex systems like lane-denying, complex item builds, day/night cycles, and high-ground vision mechanics, no two matches ever play out the same way.
3. Incredible eSports & Spectating: The game features an unmatched viewing experience with a brilliant built-in tournament client and a legacy of legendary pro matches.

The Bad:

1. Toxic Community: The in-game matchmaking is notorious for hostile players, griefers, and massive language barriers that can easily ruin a 45-minute match.
2. Brutal Learning Curve: There is no casual way to play; expect to spend your first several hundred hours just learning the absolute basics while getting crushed by smurfs.

Verdict:

9.5/10 The Most Rewarding Masterpiece You Will Ever Hate. :))

review:
Dota 2’s matchmaking is honestly fucking ridiculous. For the past 20 consecutive matches, it feels like I’m constantly being matched with players who perform horribly. Every game seems to have only 1–2 players actually trying to play properly, while the rest of the team makes the dumbest decisions imaginable.

What makes it even worse is that the enemy team somehow looks coordinated and competent almost every single game, while my team is constantly struggling. I can carry, get kills, make plays, push objectives, and do everything I possibly can, but it still ends in a loss because the rest of the team completely collapses.

I understand that not every game is supposed to be easy, and I’m not saying I should win every match. But **20 consecutive games where I constantly feel like I have to carry the entire team is beyond frustrating.** The matchmaking feels less like a fair skill-based system and more like the game is deliberately throwing completely mismatched players into the same lobby.

Dota 2 seriously needs to take a hard look at its matchmaking system and the quality of its matchmaking pools. Losing because the enemy played better is one thing. Losing repeatedly because your team is completely incapable of playing together while the enemy gets a full team of competent players is an entirely different level of frustration.

At this point, it doesn’t even feel like I’m playing against the enemy team anymore. **I’m playing against the matchmaking system and my own team at the same time.**

review:
I was introduced to DOTA in 2015
Played it on an off over the years with a little over 1200 hours only, here is my review:
1. Due to the setup of this game where people from all walks of life and ages, you often encounter especially toxic individuals often using racial slurs and provoking an argumentative environment. Feels like the biggest drawback of playing with strangers in a game that has so much potential yet, so much abuse. Perhaps not all individuals are effected by constant bullying and abuse, however, in my opinion it does impact the play of individuals.
2. The gameplay in my opinion is only designed for large screens, so if you are planning to play on a 13 inch laptop or something, just don't. The map is not customizable and stays sticky to the bottom left. Your misses will cost you your peace of mind and no one will understand. There will be lots of bullying as you will be labelled a 'noob' and constantly pushed to perform like its the olympics. ()_()
3. The reporting system is just sad. It feels like no real issue is addressed, just that you have 6 buttons to lay your observation where the action taken later is never clear. Moreover, people fake report for no reason and there is no one reviewing actual real complaints is what it feels like. Often times people have announced they are using a cheat and still they continue to play the game, I expect more responsibility from the developers of this game.
4. It felt like a space where you could make real connections and friends, a common interest such as this game is quite rare in my opinion, however after making 0 friends here in the past 11 years, I would suggest the game to change the name from 'friends' to 'contacts' as there are no people you can really call friends here. You can only become friends when you grow together, learn together and motivate each other - however, the toxicity in the majority of people usually does not allow that to happen. There is constant badgering and disappointment if you aren't a pro player. (Yep, I am talking about me when I say 'aren't a pro player'). This game has the ability to reveal the true nature of your offline friends too. :D 

I continue to play the game and try to ignore the noise, hope you do too.
Remember, kindness is a choice, you can absolutely enjoy the game without expressing your negative emotions to people, as you have NO IDEA, what they may be going through.

review: For me, this is THE definitive PVP game. It's a core interest, like a childhood hobby that becomes a lifelong, character-defining trait.
