review:
Dota 2 — A Veteran’s Perspective on What Makes It Special

I started playing Dota AllStars in 2006, when I was 17. Later, I got invited to Dota 2, and it quickly became my go-to game for most of my free time.

At my peak, I reached around 7K MMR in later part of 2016—back when Miracle- was famously the first player to reach 9K MMR in the entire world. I have also spent a ridiculous amount of time playing custom games. After all these years, I think I have played enough Dota to explain you, exactly what keeps pulling me back to it.


The Beauty of Dota 2

At its core, Dota 2 is simply an incredible strategy game.

There is an almost endless amount of depth in it: mechanical skill, decision-making, positioning, timing, resource management, drafting, itemization, map awareness, and, perhaps most importantly, the ability to turn an absolute $hitshow into a moment where everyone watching thinks:

“Wow. This guy is actually insane.”

Every game feels different. Even when you play the same hero hundreds of times, the circumstances, matchups, timings, team compositions, and decisions can completely change how the game develops.

That unpredictability is one of Dota's greatest strengths.


Of course, there is one giant problem.

Your teammates.

Ranked and Normal Dota puts four other people on your team, by the matchmaking gods of valve, and those four people can be anything from 300-IQ geniuses to the biggest flame lords ever born on planet earth. You can play your absolute best game and still watch the entire thing collapse because someone decides to do something completely incomprehensible.

And the funny thing is, the enemy team has exactly the same problem.

That is part of what makes Dota so chaotic—and sometimes so beautiful.


Dota Has Five Carries

One of the things I love most about Dota is that the concept of "carrying" is not limited to one position.

Dota essentially has five carries.

It is just a matter of when and how each player carries.

Your position 4 and position 5 might not be the ones buying the expensive late-game items, but they can absolutely carry the early game, and midgame, and even very very late game the final fight (Let's say your pos 5, 0/20/15 K/D/A WarLock making the greatest Fatal Bond of his life and dropping the golem from sky can win the final teamfight straight). A great support can create kills, secure vision, control the lane, protect the core heroes, rotate at the perfect moment, and create enough momentum that the rest of the team gets to play an easier game.

In many matches, the difference between winning and losing starts with the supports creating that early momentum.

A great Pos 4 or Pos 5 isn't simply "supporting" the carry.

They are carrying the game while helping create the farming cores become the carry.


The Meaning of Being a Carry

If you usually play Mid or Position 1 like I do, you understand what Dota means when it calls someone a "carry."

You lane well.

You farm well.

You make the right decisions.

You hit your item timings.

And eventually, you reach the part of the game where you can genuinely feel the weight of your hero.

Take Spectre, for example.

Spectre is one of those heroes where the enemy team knows exactly what they are dealing with. You don't necessarily need to be the strongest hero on the map from minute one. You need to survive, farm, reach your timings, and become the problem the enemy can no longer ignore.

Eventually, when Spectre enters a fight, the enemy doesn't just see another hero.

They only see the thing they have been afraid of for the last 30 minutes, you, the Spectre of all things.

Even a hero like Sniper, who is notoriously fragile, can become terrifying when played correctly. Dota gives you a huge amount of freedom in how you build your hero. There isn't always one fixed item build that you blindly follow every game. 

Yeah, I bought Abyssal Blade for Sniper just to counter Doom jumping on me with his BKB on, I was doomed for sure but I rightclicked him to death. He couldnt even hit me with his right click becuase Doom has very bad attack speed and his cast swing is very long. Sniper has machine gun tier attack speed + bash from Abyssal + your headshot push back passive to win one of the most unfair manfights. Item might be melee focused but you can do $hit like this if situation calls for it. Free your mind and just do it, it usually works :)

You can adapt.

You can buy defensive items because you're being jumped.

You can build damage because you love biggg numbers.

You can completely change your build because the enemy lineup demands it.

That freedom is a huge part of what makes Dota feel like Dota.


Why I Prefer Dota's Version of Carrying

I have also played League of Legends—I somehow reached Master—but the concept of carrying feels very different there.

In League, depending on the situation, you can feel incredibly vulnerable. An assassin, burst mage, or even another damage dealer can sometimes erase you incredibly quickly. Take Jhin or Jinx for example, you can blow up in one second if someone touches you and they click their keyboard correctly in sequence. You are gone, in a bloody 1-2 second at max.


Dota feels different.

The game gives you more tools to respond to the situation. Your hero isn't necessarily locked into one build or one predetermined role. You can change your itemization, positioning, playstyle, and priorities depending on what is happening on the map. Even if you play very squishy hero, you don't blow up quick if you farmed as a carry player.

And when you finally become that late-game carry, you can feel it.

The enemy team feels your presence.

They have to think about where you are.

They have to consider your items.

They have to change how they initiate.

They have to decide whether they can kill you before you destroy them.

And with a hero like Spectre, sometimes the biggest threat isn't even where you are.

It's knowing that you can join the teamfight from anywhere.

You started the early game with survival horror movie to become the raid boss at the end.


The $hitshows Are Part of the Experience

Dota can be frustrating as hell.

You will have teammates who make you question whether they have ever touched a keyboard before.

You will lose games that you absolutely should have won.

You will have games where you are playing perfectly and still feel completely helpless.

But every once in a while, something magical happens.

You are 10,000 gold behind.

Your lanes are destroyed.

Your teammates are arguing.

The enemy team is laughing.

Everyone thinks the game is over.

And somehow, you find a way.

One smoke.

One high-ground defense.

One perfectly timed buyback.

One insane teamfight.

One player making the right decision at exactly the right second.

Suddenly, the impossible comeback becomes real.

Those are the games you remember.

Not the easy 25-minute stomps.

Not the games where everything went according to plan.

The unforgettable ones are the absolute disasters where you somehow turned a losing game into a victory.


Final Thoughts

After playing Dota for roughly two decades, I still think it is one of the best competitive games ever made.

It is frustrating, complicated, unfair, beautiful, ridiculous, strategic, mechanical, and sometimes completely insane.

You can spend 60 minutes in a game experiencing every possible emotion a video game can give you.

You can hate your teammates.

You can hate yourself.

You can hate the enemy team or one specific enemy.

You can swear you are never playing again.

And then you make one incredible play, turn the entire game around, destroy the enemy Ancient, and immediately queue for another match.

That's Dota 2.

The game doesn't guarantee you a good experience every time.

But when everything comes together—when the strategy, mechanics, teamwork, adaptation, and sheer chaos align—it can give you some of the most unforgettable 60 minutes you will ever spend in gaming.

Returned to Dota 2 after some years. Mostly because of nostalgia. I don't like the state of the game
- Heroes are too hard to kill, even the supports have a lot of HP. Some heroes even have 2k HP in the first 10 minutes while even some carry heroes have 2k HP after 15-20 minutes, which is kinda dumb.
- Too many hero and item reworks. Tried to read them all but it's too boring. 100+ heroes and 200+ items and how they all interact with each other and so on.
- Everyone seems to be able to farm items no matter what.
- Arcade is not working at all: No servers are found, down for maintenance, etc.
- Matchmaking takes a lot of time at certain hours. You would think that such a game would have not that long of a queue for matchmaking. (Unranked, All Pick, 9-10 AM on a Sunday)
- Matchmaking is the worst that I've seen in any game: Teams are totally unbalanced, I don't know how the rating is being calculated. Rather than being paired with players my skill level, I am getting paired with people with thousand of games.
- Parties are able to queue into matchmaking solo queue. It seems that parties of 2-3 people are able to queue on solo and coordinate better that 5 individual people would on their own, which again leads to frustration about the pairings and the team.
- Always getting queued with certain nationalities that start spamming the all chat in their language. And also the chat wheel messages. I have no clue why chat wheel messages spam are considered ok by valve. They are just annoying.
- I have always played mid or safe lane carry. I am forced by the matchmaking system to play hard lane every game, or queue as support in order to get "tokens" so i can actually queue as mid or safe laner. Why am I forced to play as a role that I don't want to play as and that I don't have any knowledge on how to play it? This makes the games not enjoyable at all for me. I want to be able to pick the hero that I want and play how I want, not be forced into a role and a hero that I don't want to play.
- I picked Broodmother once and when getting into a game I briefly looked at the abilities and they were reworked entirely. Instantiable hunger is now the first skill, spawn broodlings is the ultimate, and spider web gives no invisibility. I don't know who came up with this stuff, but it's embarrassing.
- Players grief as usual. They throw the game hard or pick heroes they have no business playing (probably due to the matchmaking system).
- They made the map bigger with more neutrals camps, but still haven't fixed the 6 item max slot issue. You see time and time again, even in the international, that heroes have gold to make more items, but they are capped at 6 items. Why not 8 or 9? or more? It should have been the first limitation that was removed or increased. A lot of games you would need 1-2 extra items to be able to deal with enemy heroes. Maybe you would need Linken's, or BKB, or Hex, but you aren't able to have them equipped because of the item slots.
- The nostalgia quickly went away and I remember why I quit in the first place. The toxic community (been reporting players every single game and it says action was taken but I'm getting tired of it), the constant reworks of items and heroes, the matchmaking system, the arcade not working, and so on.
- I have no clue what new players are supposed to feel when they start playing Dota 2, as this was confusing for me, I can't imagine how they must be feeling when they play.

It's not something that I enjoy playing anymore. I gave it 2 weeks but that's it.

review:
Dota 2 is honestly one of the most unique and challenging games I’ve ever played. At first, the game can feel extremely overwhelming because there are so many heroes, items, abilities, mechanics, and strategies to learn. But once you start understanding how everything works, the game becomes incredibly rewarding.

What I love most about Dota 2 is that no two matches feel exactly the same. Every game can play out differently depending on the heroes, players, item choices, and decisions made throughout the match. There are so many different ways to approach a game, and even after playing for a long time, there is always something new to learn.

The hero variety is also amazing. Whether you prefer playing aggressively, supporting your teammates, farming, pushing objectives, or making strategic plays, there’s probably a hero that fits your playstyle. The item system also gives you a lot of freedom to adapt your build depending on what is happening in the match.

Of course, Dota 2 isn't perfect. Some matches can be extremely frustrating, especially when your team isn't communicating or when everything seems to go wrong. You might lose a game that you thought you had already won, or make one small mistake that completely changes the outcome. But that's also part of what makes winning so satisfying.

Dota 2 has a very high skill ceiling, and that’s probably one of its biggest strengths. You can play hundreds or even thousands of hours and still discover new strategies and improve your decision-making. It rewards patience, teamwork, game knowledge, and practice.

Overall, Dota 2 is definitely not a game for everyone, especially if you want something simple and casual. But if you're willing to spend time learning it, it can provide an incredible amount of entertainment. The learning curve is steep, the matches can be chaotic, and sometimes you will question your life choices after a bad game—but somehow, you still queue for another one.

10/10. Would lose another ranked game and blame the Internet again. 😂

review:
I’ve been playing Dota 2 since 2013.

No other game is as fun as Dota 2, but the inverse is also true: no other game has given me this much frustration and grief. I have invested many hours of my life into this game, and I do not regret it.

I've made genuine connections through this game that turned into real-life friendships. Ultimately, this game is best played with friends. In its current state, Dota 2 needs to be friendlier to new players. I can enjoy the game given I have 6,000+ hours across various accounts, but the steep initial investment pushes people away from wanting to learn.

Dota 2 is a fantastic game, and I highly recommend it. Just know that if you want to play, it requires a huge time investment—one that is made much easier when you play with a friend. Once that learning curve is over, you'll start seeing yourself improve and get a satisfaction that few other games can match.

review: Dota 2 is good. Not “pretty good,” not “fun for a few hundred hours,” but the kind of good that rewires your brain and makes every other game feel like a tutorial with training wheels. The depth is absurd. Every hero, every item, every timing window, every fog-of-war mind game stacks on top of itself until you’re sitting there at 3 a.m. calculating whether that second Blink Dagger is greedy or genius. The skill ceiling is so high it might as well be in orbit. No two games feel the same. One match you’re stomping with perfect vision control and the next you’re getting dumpstered by a five-man smoke that you somehow still respect because the execution was filthy. The map is alive. The items are decisions. The drafting is chess with extra steps and more salt. It’s the purest expression of competitive multiplayer that still lets you be a complete degenerate while doing it. That’s why it’s good. That’s why people still queue after a decade-plus of this nonsense.My favorite character is Hoodwink. Full stop. I main her. I spam her. I think about her between games. She’s a tiny squirrel girl with a crossbow, a bush, and the most unreasonably perfect design in the entire hero pool. The way she moves is criminal. That little hop, the way her tail flicks when she’s idle, the smug little smirk in her voice lines—she’s pure concentrated cute weaponized into a mid-to-late game monster. Her model is small and compact in the best way. The acorn shield, the sharp little ears, the way her cloak sits on those shoulders, the playful bounce in her animations when she lands a Sharpshooter. She’s adorable in a way that feels intentional and slightly dangerous. The kind of cute that makes you want to keep her in the tree line forever, watching her set up that perfect bush for the next scavenger strike. Everything about her is cute: the size, the energy, the cheeky personality, the way she casually ruins someone’s day with a 1200-range stun while looking like she just stole your last snack and is proud of it. I love her. A little too much, probably. She’s the one hero I never get tired of looking at.Ranked is a different story. The actual game is still great, but the ranked experience is garbage for one very specific reason: everyone mutes me the second they hear me open my mouth. I’m Black. That’s it. That’s the whole problem. Voice chat turns into radio silence the moment I speak. Text chat gets the same treatment. People would rather play 4v5 information blackout than hear a single call from me. It doesn’t matter if the call is correct. It doesn’t matter if I just saved the game with a perfect Acorn Shot. Muted. Every. Single. Time. The ranked ladder is already full of tilted randoms and ego drafting, but the instant, automatic mute treatment because of how I sound makes the whole thing feel broken on a personal level. You can still climb if you’re good enough and mute yourself first, but the social layer of the mode is just dead on arrival for me. It’s the one part of Dota that actually feels bad instead of hard.Everything else? Still the best game on Steam. The updates keep coming. The mechanics stay deep. And Hoodwink is still out here being the cutest, most unfairly charming little menace in the entire roster. I’ll keep queueing. Just don’t expect me to unmute.

review:
A lot of people have said it, but valve won't listen.  The integrity reporting system makes the game unplayable.  I could feel myself burning out of this game and today seems to be the day.  The inmates are running the Asylum when it comes to reporting people.  When you are low tier player you get reported for anything and everything. Its impossible to climb out of. They could make this cool by doing the adult thing and just get rid of reporting system and state if you don't like someone mute them.  Instead we have East Berlin/USSR silencing/reporting system in place. 

Probably the worst thing to me was actually the hero changes over time that has made them completely un-fun. I enjoyed the facets, which were removed. I felt many of them had their place and also made the game more balanced because people had a much more diverse meta to choose from.  

They completely destroyed Dazzle in the worst way possible over time. They took one of the coolest concepts, spell cooldown reduction, and just got rid of it.  The hero still has the ability to stack armor on allies...but they removed the utlimate that allowed you to stack armor.  How does this make any sense? You get no spell cooldown reduction and now have an ultimate where enemies can see you even in the fog...? The hero has zero ability to farm, but is just a sterile lame hero.  The hero has been 'ok' in the patch, but it doesn't matter its completely sterile and boring.  You can place well timed save and thats it.  I went into detail on this to say that valve has done this with the game generally.  Nerfed heros to the ground removed core concepts from heros and made the game sterile.  Its not a balancing issue, its boredom and antithetical to the heros. It doesn't feel like you can outmeta people through items, skill tree, or raw skill it comes down to teammates, smurfs, and hero choices.  One fight goes wrong at 20 min and the game is just over.

Overall there is just a lot of evidence they  have stopped caring about the players and the game.  The game is unidimensional right now.  In the current "candystore" I can't use any of my candy because every single role is some treasure or skin from 2013.  I've probably roled 30-40x and not found single useful thing.  They have so much of this where they hand out 'prizes' that is worse than looking through a dumpster.

review:
Here I am again, playing Dota 2 after being a Dota 1 player for several years myself. The community is pretty different, and so is the way people approach the game. I’ve supported most of the new patches and heroes, BUT some of them are broken as hell (we’ve seen them in the last and most recent TIs).
As always, Dota is a game of constantly changing metas, patches, and new events. The new events that allow people to get cosmetics and other customizable items are kind of the GACHA part of the game at the moment. I understand that for some players it’s part of the business, while for others it’s just collecting. I don’t know if I enjoy that part TOO MUCH, but the nostalgia is definitely there.
There’s a long road ahead to truly understand the map and learn how to grow with Dota 2, but I would recommend Dota 2 over ANY OTHER MOBA on the market in 2026.

PLAY IT. LEARN IT. GROW. USE YOUR HEAD. THINK.

This is a game that pushes you to THINK OR SUCK... it’s up to you.

review:
I thought *Dota 2* was just another popular MOBA that everyone played because it was competitive.

I was wrong.

At first, it looks complicated. There are dozens of heroes, hundreds of abilities, items everywhere, and enough terminology to make you wonder if you accidentally enrolled in a university course.

But somewhere along the way, you start understanding it.

And then you're in trouble.

The gameplay is incredibly deep. Every match can turn into a completely different experience depending on the heroes, players, builds, decisions, and the thousand tiny mistakes everyone makes along the way.

The first few games can feel overwhelming. Then you learn one thing. Then another. Eventually, you realize you've spent hundreds of hours learning a game that still has more to teach you.

The best part is how much your decisions matter.

One good team fight can change everything. One terrible decision can throw an entire match. Sometimes you make the perfect play and feel like a genius.

Sometimes you walk into the enemy team and immediately question every decision you've ever made.

I've played games with simpler mechanics, easier learning curves, and much less stress.

I don't remember most of them.

I'll remember *Dota 2*.

Some games are competitive because they want you to win.

*Dota 2* is competitive because it wants you to become obsessed with figuring out why you lost.

And then queue again.

100% recommended.

review:
[i]Dota 2 is a 5v5 moba strategy game that I have been playing for~
Oh... 
Oh, no...[/i]

[h1]Flows[/h1][list]
[*]Dota 2 rewards reflexes... But it rewards strategic thinking much more. And the skill ceiling of strategic thinking in a game with so many variables is (team compositions, item combinations, map positioning, etc.) nearly endless.
[*]The whole game is focused on mechanics. Going faster by following the flow of the rivers, having no vision of higher ground areas, most of the terrain obstacles being trees that you can destroy with extremely basic items or hills that you can pass over with abilities or items, there is a day and night cycle with the later giving you increased movement speed but reduced visibility... Dota 2's map is far more than a flat board that might as well be background, it's a core part of the game.
[*]Speaking of, the map is BIG, especially compared to other mobas. Traversing it takes time, and this is very much intentional. Map awareness is one of the most important skills a player should have. And I suck at it.
[*]Over 100 heroes to choose, each doing something extremely unique. You will get no copy-pasted characters here, despite the huge roster (and unlike "some other popular mobas"). There is a hero that becomes deadly in the night but is weak during the day, one that focuses on brainwashing jungle creeps to fight for him, another that becomes stronger in water terrains, another that destroys trees as part of his core mechanics and on and on. The gameplay variety is fantastic.
[*]In fact the mechanics of each hero are so unique, that the interactions between their various moves and the items they can buy are completely chaotic and infinitely entertaining. In general I love the sandbox approach Dota takes with its individual hero/team builds. There is a series called "Dota WTF" on YouTube that releases weekly, showing compilations of absurd in-game interactions recorded by players, hilarious more often than not. At the time this review is written [i]it is at episode 646...[/i]
[*]Every hero is strong in his own right, but certain heroes are simply above the rest in terms of power/flexibility. The "reason" they are above the rest is the same mechanical complexity that makes them challenging to control in the first place. Invoker is the most obvious example (a character with 9 different ultis, formed through your QWE basic ability combinations), but he is far from the only one.
[*]Heroes are strong in what they do, but hardly anyone has an all-purposes complete kit. Each hero has built-in weaknesses to their arsenal (e.g. no defensive options/slow movement speed/heavy mana reliance, etc. etc.), and a smart opponent will exploit them. You will need to take yours into account and either supplement them through item builds, or choose specific team combinations. It is not unusual for games to be decided before they even start, by which team has the better synergy. 
[*]Visually, each hero is unique (audibly as well actually, the voice acting is fantastic). This obviously includes a plethora of babes, the hottest of which being Templar Assassin, an Arab-dancer-themed babe with Psylocke's abilities (you are of course allowed to prefer another female character as your favorite. It's just that you're wrong.) The more monsterous designs are the highlight though (and they have the best cosmetics).
[*]The cosmetics are not single skins, but parts of skins, that you can combine as you like. You will either be playing Barbie, activating Polymerization, or enacting your inner doctor Frankenstein. Other cosmetics called "personas" and "arcanas" even completely redesign the characters from the base model.  On that note, a lot of the cosmetics are designed by players, viewable in the game's Steam workshop at any time, and you can actually vote which ones you like.
[*]Budget-wise, cosmetics are really affordable, with lootbox releases being infrequent.
[*]Cosmetics include UI elements. Map skins, announcer packs, custom UIs and many more. A player who uses one of these can freely share it with the rest of his team, applied in the same session instantly.
[*]The dark fantasy aesthetics really do it for me. Dota doesn't aim for realistic OR cartoony graphics, in the style LoL does, but rather for intentionally edgy 3D visuals. And it works.
[*]Players can program crazy variants of the standard Dota build, including new maps, characters or even gamestyles, and then share them through the "Arcade" tab of the game. Currently I am watching a single-player roguelike called "Emberfall", while a football-themed variant was trending last week. The engine freedom Valve provides with Dota (and all its games in general) is absurd.
[*]The developers really go balls to the wall with the major patches. Absolutely no rule is set in stone, and every game aspect is liable to be experimented on. I wouldn't call it so much "evolving" as "mutating", but it's still very entertaining and great at maintaining your interest.[/list]

[h1]Flaws[/h1][list]
[*]I am really not a fan of the direction Dota's storytelling has taken. The Marvel-style humor & Rick and Morty style of self-awareness is a very ill fit for Dota's dark fantasy aesthetics and cosmically horrifying original lore.
[*]Frankly the map could use a lot more interactions. I was a huge fan of Heroes of the Storm and its fantastic map-objective approach, and I wish Dota would take more ques for it.
[*]While there are some mildly fanservice-y outfits for the girls, Valve is intentionally being conservative with them, and that's a shame.
[*]The lack of a proper hero ban system is really hurting the game. Some heroes are banned randomly at the start of every match, but, objectively this should have been the players' choice instead of an RNG result.
[*]In general, RNG is far more prevalent in Dota than it should have been. Ranged attacks to someone on higher ground have a 25% miss chance, or so the game says, because it's quite common to miss 5+ shots in a row. An Ogre Magi might trigger his QWE kit once each... Or each of them might trigger 4 times in the span of 2 seconds. Items often have a chance to trigger their attack modifiers, rather than having them guaranteed. I get that "some" RNG is supposed to be a part of it, but hitting someone 10+ hits with a Spirit Breaker and not triggering a single bash can lead to some very understandable screen punches.
[*]Items are generally separated into early game items, mid game items and late game items. The vast majority of early and mid game permanent items are used as materials for some late game item, essentially evolving into them. Unfortunately that is not the case for some of them, including 2 out of the 4 evolutions of your boots, an aura buffing item called "Vladimir's Offering" and many others. Therefore the optimal play is to simply sell those items in the late game and buy something entirely new. The problem is you liked those items, and would very much prefer to have an evolved version of them instead of just erasing them from your arsenal.
[*]The isometric view makes navigating trees really difficult. Oftentimes it looks like there is a path for you, but there isn't, resulting in your character taking a route he really shouldn't have taken. When you are being chased, that usually results in your death.
[*]Completely random disconnections are not too uncommon, along with a variety of other technical issues, such as the client having trouble synching with the coordinator.
[*]At some point, you will run out of Ukraine death jokes for all the Russians infesting European servers, despite having a dedicated server of their own. Communications issues arise, since they never speak English.[/list]

[b]Thumps up, go play it and get humbled. Dota 2 is a fantastic moba, with heavy emphasis on strategy, fantastic audiovisual design, customization options and RNG elements that encourage you to learn new slurs.

[b]Valve no longer respects your time or patience.[/b]

[hr]

[h2]Dota 2[/h2]

Dota’s biggest problem for me is the [b]behavior and communication system.[/b]

The idea behind punishing genuinely toxic players is completely reasonable. The problem is that the system often feels incapable of distinguishing between someone who is actually abusive and someone who simply had a bad game.

You can underperform, have a terrible match, make repeated mistakes, or simply become the target of frustrated teammates, and suddenly you can be [b]mass-reported.[/b] The consequences can include losing access to communication features, even though [b]poor performance and toxic behavior are two completely different things.[/b]

That is incredibly frustrating in a game such as Dota that relies so heavily on team-play. People are going to have bad games. People are going to make mistakes. Sometimes you’re going to get completely [i]shit on[/i] and outplayed.

[b]None of those things should automatically make someone a candidate for losing their ability to communicate.[/b]

What makes the system worse is the lack of transparency.

You literally [b]cannot get help from Steam or Dota support.[/b] They will not help you. I have tried multiple times to find out why my score has fallen so much, only to get the most generic copy-and-paste replies.

So good luck fixing the issue.

Good luck finding out what you actually did wrong.

Good luck figuring out what you can actually do to resolve the situation.

When the obviously automated system gets something wrong — [b]which it can and does[/b] — there is absolutely no way for the player to challenge that decision, or even find out why the decision was made in the first place.

[hr]

Dota is already an extremely demanding game.

You have to learn hundreds of interactions, understand constantly changing strategies, coordinate with four other players, and deal with the enormous amount of information being thrown at you every match.

The last thing the game needs is a behavior system that makes players afraid that one bad stretch of games could affect their ability to communicate or even just play in general.

And that's before getting into:

[list]
[*]Griefing
[*]Smurfing
[*]Matchmaking frustrations
[*]And the fact that these problems have existed for far too long
[/list]

I don't expect Valve to eliminate every toxic player from Dota.

[b]That's impossible.[/b]

I expect the systems designed to deal with those players to be [b]accurate, transparent, and fair.[/b]

[hr]

[h2]Counter-Strike 2[/h2]

I know this is a review for Dota 2, but I have just had it [b]up to here[/b] with every aspect of Valve.

So let's just get into it.

Counter-Strike has a completely different set of problems, but the underlying issue is similar:

[b]Players have increasingly little confidence in the systems that are supposed to protect the competitive experience.[/b]

[h3]Cheating[/h3]

Cheating is obviously the biggest example.

For a competitive shooter where the entire experience depends on players believing that the people they're playing against are legitimate, confidence in anti-cheat is absolutely fundamental.

When players repeatedly encounter suspicious players and don't feel confident that those players will actually be caught, it damages the entire competitive environment — and leads to even more hackers.

If a completely innocent and legitimate player queues up for 50 matches, and out of those 50, even 10 of them had someone hacking, this leaves a small wedge in some players' minds that the only way to combat them is to [b]hack themselves.[/b]

Now what do we have?

[h3]A hacker producer.[/h3]

Every 100 new players that attempt to get into CS2 will either give up after 10 games, or succumb to hacking just to keep up.

[b]That is how you destroy the integrity of a competitive game.[/b]

[hr]

Then there are smurfs, griefers, matchmaking frustrations, and the overall inconsistency of the competitive experience.

Counter-Strike doesn't need to be perfect.

No anti-cheat system will ever catch every cheater immediately, and no matchmaking system will create perfectly balanced games every time.

But players need to believe that Valve is [b]aggressively fighting these problems.[/b]

When it becomes blatantly obvious that the developers behind the scenes do not care, why should the players?

Every suspicious death becomes another reason to become part of the problem, or to wonder whether the match was legitimate in the first place.

[b]That's incredibly damaging to a competitive game.[/b]

And once again, Valve has the resources to do better.

They have the resources to do [b]so, so much better.[/b]

Counter-Strike is one of the biggest competitive shooters in the world.

This isn't some obscure game with a tiny development team trying to survive.

Valve has an enormous amount of money, infrastructure, data, and experience behind it.

[hr]

[h2]The Bigger Problem With Valve[/h2]

This is what bothers me most about both games.

The problems aren't necessarily identical, but the pattern feels identical:

[h3][b]Valve seems increasingly comfortable letting fundamental problems exist as long as the games remain profitable.[/b][/h3]

And why wouldn't they be?

People continue spending hundreds or even thousands of dollars on cosmetics.

Steam continues generating enormous amounts of revenue.

Dota and Counter-Strike continue attracting massive player bases.

[b]There is very little financial incentive to completely overhaul systems that players constantly complain about when those same players continue spending money anyway.[/b]

I want Valve to invest in the foundations of these games.

I want Dota's behavior systems to be more transparent and better at distinguishing toxicity from simply playing badly.

I want Counter-Strike's competitive integrity systems to inspire confidence rather than suspicion.

I want matchmaking, reporting, anti-cheat, communication systems, and moderation to feel like they were designed around [b]protecting the player experience[/b] rather than simply automating problems away.

[hr]

Valve built its reputation by making games that felt years ahead of everyone else.

That's why it's so disappointing to see two of its most important games reach a point where so many players feel ignored.

[h2]The golden age of Valve is long past.[/h2]

But maybe it doesn't have to stay that way.

[b]But as long as players continue handing Valve money regardless of how these games are maintained, I don't see much reason for the company to change.[/b]

[h3]GG, Valve. gg.[/h3]

Dota is the purest love-hate relationship I've ever had with a game. Every match somehow leaves you frustrated, exhausted, and still wanting to queue again. One game you get the best teammates ever and everything just works, then the next game you get the kind of team that makes you hate the match, hate the game, and for a few minutes, hate everyone in it.

Losing can feel miserable, winning can feel euphoric, and both still make you want to play one more.

With friends though, this game can be absolutely amazing and some of the best fun you'll have. So for newcomers, expect psychological torture, countless hours of your life gone, an unhealthy attachment to a game you'll swear you hate, while still being one of the best competitive experiences you'll ever have.

And at the time of writing this, The International 2026 begins tomorrow. All my wishes to Falcons to lift the Aegis!

review:
Dota 2: The Best Digital Anger Management Test Ever Made

Hours Played: 2.8
Rating: 0/10 - Will play again tonight.

If you have ever wondered what it feels like to pay zero dollars to be verbally berated in four different languages simultaneously, Valve has created the masterwork for you.

The Onboarding Experience: The tutorial teaches you how to move your character and hit a couple of creep creeps. The actual game then immediately drops you into a match against a 12 year old mid-laner who plays Invoker with the finger precision of a concert pianist and the temperament of a distressed badger.

Team Chemistry: Your team will invariably consist of a hard support who rushes a Divine Rapier, an offlaner who disconnected during hero selection, and a carry who spends 40 minutes farming the jungle only to die instantly in the final teamfight because they were typing an essay in all chat.

Matchmaking: Breathtakingly efficient. It accurately pairs you with four teammates who seem to be playing on trackpads using dial-up internet from inside a running blender.

Pros:

It is completely free, meaning you lose no actual money, just your hair, your sleep schedule, and your faith in humanity.

Incredible sound design, the pinging noise will follow you into your dreams.

Cons:

Requires a functioning nervous system, which it promptly destroys.

Verdict:
10/10 mechanics, 0/10 mental health impact. Download it if you feel like your life currently has too little stress and way too much inner peace.

review: Wasn't really into MOBA's before this game. As far as MOBA's go, this game is best of the best. Every win feels very rewarding, and each loss has something to learn from it. There is so much depth in each part of the game, and it's very rare for any game, let alone a MOBA with 127 heroes to feel balanced. Between patches there are def some heroes that are stronger than others, but for 90% of the player base it doesn't really matter. Game knowledge and skill is way more important than what heroes you play that are strong at the moment. Every dota player has experienced being completely destroyed by some low tier hero that was played to the absolute maximum. The game isn't restrictive like other MOBA's. You can truly make some wild and wacky stuff work as long as you execute great. It is very rare for the correct play to be building the exact same items every game on a hero. Each game is dynamic, and you have to respond to what heroes and items the enemies have, trying to do the same thing every time just wont work. Overall, this is probably one of the best balanced, high skill ceiling MOBA's there is.

review:
This game is one of the most aggressively addictive and psychologically miserable designs I have ever encountered.

Dota 2 doesn’t just have a toxic community — it is practically engineered to produce one. The character designs, voice lines, tipping system, taunts, and hyper-competitive environment constantly encourage players to provoke, boast, humiliate, insult, and tilt each other. Then everyone acts surprised when the atmosphere becomes unbearable.

The ranking system, MVP system, and progression mechanics are equally absurd. You can have an amazing game and accomplish something genuinely impressive, yet the game’s arbitrary systems can make it feel like none of it mattered. Get a rampage with Techies, for example, and somehow the progression system can barely acknowledge what you just did. The whole thing often feels less like measuring performance and more like rolling dice with a UI attached.

And then comes the final masterpiece of incompetence: the endless updates. Valve seems to have developed the pathological need to change something simply because they feel they have to change something. Mechanics that were perfectly fine get needlessly redesigned, unnecessary systems are introduced, then later “fixed” when they inevitably make things worse. It is an endless cycle of changing things for the sake of changing them and then pretending the subsequent cleanup is meaningful development.

Dota 2 is an incredible example of how a technically sophisticated game can become an absolutely exhausting experience through its own design philosophy. It feels like a game that has been deliberately optimized to keep you addicted, frustrated, competitive, and angry — and then offers you another match before you have time to ask yourself why you are still playing.

At some point, you have to admire the achievement: they managed to turn a game into a punishment loop and convince millions of people to volunteer for it.

review:
(Recommended, with the same enthusiasm one recommends a particularly involved religion)

There is a moment, roughly four hundred hours into your relationship with Dota 2, when you look up from the screen, notice that it is dark outside, that several meals have gone unmentioned to your body, and that you have just spent eleven minutes arguing with four strangers about whether someone called "xXx_PudgeGod_xXx" should have bought a Black King Bar. It is at this moment that you understand, with the calm clarity of a man who has seen the Total Perspective Vortex and lived, that Dota 2 is not so much a video game as it is a weather system that has learned to hold a grudge.1

It begins innocently enough. Somewhere, a small green shop sells you boots. This seems reasonable. Boots are a known quantity; humanity has understood boots for some time. But then you are asked to choose from over a hundred heroes, each possessing between four and infinity abilities, several of which do not do what their names suggest and at least one of which summons a second, smaller version of yourself to die on your behalf, which, if you think about it for too long, and you will have time, because games run to the fifty-minute mark as a matter of house pride, raises troubling questions about identity that Douglas Adams would have handled with a towel and Terry Pratchett would have handled by introducing a footnote longer than the original sentence.2

The game does not want you to win. This should be stated plainly, because the tutorial is too polite to say it. The game wants you to almost win, forever, in ever-more-elaborate ways, the way the universe wants a soufflé to almost rise. You will lose games you dominated. You will win games you spent apologising for. Somewhere a small number called MMR will go up or down by an amount so precisely calibrated to feel meaningless that you will nonetheless stare at it the way sailors once stared at the horizon, looking for weather.
And yet.

And yet there is a particular, specific joym, not happiness, exactly, happiness is too small and well-behaved a word, that arrives when five people who have never met, who do not speak the same language, who are frankly a little worried about each other's life choices, click four buttons in the correct order and a fight that was unwinnable becomes, briefly, gloriously winnable. For about six seconds, Dota 2 makes perfect sense, the way the universe is said to make perfect sense to people right before they get flattened by an unlikely bus. Then someone facechecks a bush and it is over, and you queue again, because you are only human, and humans are the sort of species that, having been burned by fire, invent a game about being burned by fire, and play it every night for a decade.

review:
The current game's integrity system encourages people to unfairly report each other, not for genuinely disrespectful behavior, but simply for using vulgar language, even in a positive way. Sometimes you can get reports for a simple request, if teammates are having a bad day. I don't know why they started rewarding integrity for successful reports—it's like those memes about the Soviet Union, where everyone reported on each other "just in case, for no reason, just because."

This is an incredibly inept system, worse than if there was no integrity system at all, like in 2013. I recommend review-bombing this game until the developers say something about their own mistakes.

Until then, I'm deleting the game and don't recommend anyone play this disgrace. It's better not to play a competitive game at all than to be afraid to say anything, especially a non-offensive, polite call.

I thought the community would kill this game, but in the end, the developers decided to kill it themselves, giving the worst part of the playerbase tools to pressure all other players, allowing them to ruin the game for absolutely everyone else.

I'm behaving better in-game now than ever, which has nothing to do with the behaviour system, but with my maturation. Paradoxically, I'm getting more penalties than ever for literally nothing, sometimes even for celebrating my team's success. I'm left with no emotions from the game other than the monstrous injustice felt by both myself and many other people who can't communicate in voice chat, but don't seem nearly as insane as the people who report them.

I think it's because the most reasonable players have stopped reporting.

review:
I installed Dota 2 expecting a competitive multiplayer game.

What I received was an unpaid apprenticeship in human suffering.

There are games where you learn mechanics, improve your reflexes, develop strategies, and eventually become better than you were before. Dota takes a more ambitious approach. It attempts to reconstruct your entire personality from the ground up.

You begin with confidence.

You select a hero. You buy your starting items. You walk towards the lane with the quiet optimism of someone who has absolutely no idea what is about to happen.

Ten minutes later, your Russian teammate is furiously typing because you didn't rotate.

You don't know what he is saying, but you understand the emotional meaning.

Apparently you have committed an international crime.

This is one of Dota's greatest features: the extraordinary diversity of human personalities you encounter. There is always one player who has been waiting their entire life for this particular match and will personally investigate every mistake you have made since the moment you installed Steam.

Miss one last hit?

Reported.

Die to a gank?

Reported.

Buy the wrong item?

Reported.

Exist in the same geographical region as Russia?

Probably reported.

And yet, somehow, the same people who are threatening to uninstall the game, abandon the match, and report the entire team will still be playing another game approximately fourteen seconds after the Ancient explodes.

Then there are the specialists.

The carry who has spent 38 minutes farming and suddenly announces that the team needs to "play around me."

The support who has purchased approximately 14 wards but has placed all of them in locations where absolutely nothing has ever happened.

The mid player who dies twice and immediately begins constructing a legal case against the position 4.

The offlaner who has been missing since minute six.

And the mysterious player who says "trust me" immediately before doing something that results in four deaths.

Somehow, despite all of this, you continue playing.

Because every once in a while, Dota produces a moment so perfectly coordinated that you briefly understand why millions of people willingly subject themselves to this game.

A smoke.

A perfect initiation.

Five enemy heroes caught.

Spells flying everywhere.

Your entire team screaming in celebration.

The enemy Ancient falls.

For a brief and beautiful moment, everyone loves each other.

Then you queue again.

And this is where Dota becomes truly impressive.

It doesn't matter how many times you swear that this is your last game. Dota has perfected the psychological art of making you believe that the next match will be different.

It won't.

The next match will contain another Russian who is somehow both your teammate and your sworn enemy.

Another person will type "gg" at minute eight.

Someone will disconnect.

Someone will buy an item that makes no sense.

Someone will blame you for something that happened on the opposite side of the map.

And you will sit there at 2:17 in the morning thinking:

"Surely we can win the next one."

Dota 2 is not a game you finish.

It is a cycle you enter.

You lose.

You blame your team.

Your team blames you.

You promise never to play again.

You queue again.

You win.

You experience an indescribable feeling of superiority.

You queue again.

You lose.

And somewhere in the distance, a Russian player is typing something in all chat that is probably not appropriate for this review.

10/10.

Terrible game.

See you tomorrow.

review:
**⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 1/10 — I hate this game**

Dota 2 is not a game.

It is a psychological experiment conducted on people who willingly click **“Find Match”** despite knowing exactly what is going to happen.

And somehow… I love it.

The gameplay is incredible. There is always something new to learn. Every hero can feel completely different, every match can turn into a 60-minute movie, and sometimes you pull off a play so beautiful that you briefly believe you are the greatest Dota player alive.

Then your support walks into five enemies alone.

Dies.

Buys back.

Does it again.

Types **“team?”**

Peak Dota.

The best part is that you can spend 45 minutes carefully farming, warding, smoking, controlling Roshan and executing the perfect teamfight…

…only for a guy named **xX_Destroyer420_Xx** to buy a Divine Rapier and run directly into the enemy fountain.

**-25 MMR.**

Beautiful.

10/10.

I love the complexity, the strategy, the ridiculous heroes and the fact that literally anything can happen.

I hate the matchmaking, griefers, smurfs, disconnects and that mysterious teammate who suddenly becomes a professional philosopher after dying once:

**“gg.”**

Overall:

**80% amazing game.
20% emotional damage.
100% addiction.**

Would recommend.

Would I recommend playing ranked at 2 AM?

Absolutely not.

Will I do it tonight?

**Yes.**

Now please upvote this review. I need at least one victory today.

review:
After thousands of hours in Dota 2, I think I’ve finally discovered the best advice I can give to any new player:

Don’t play Dota 2.

Seriously. Go play League of Legends, ROV, Mobile Legends, or literally any other MOBA where the developers still appear to remember that their game has players.

Valve’s approach to smurfing is honestly impressive — not because they’ve solved it, but because somehow, after all these years, smurf accounts are still being created, boosted, sold, and thrown into lower-ranked matches like they’re part of the official matchmaking experience.

Maybe smurfing isn’t a problem anymore.

Maybe it’s a feature.

And if you think reaching a higher rank will finally improve your experience, congratulations — Valve has apparently been working hard to make that worse too.

Just look at what has happened at the very top of the ladder. When even Rank 1 players can watch their rank collapse in ways that make the entire system look ridiculous, you really have to admire Valve’s dedication to making sure nobody feels safe — not beginners, not veterans, not even the best players in the game.

Equal opportunity suffering.

Beautiful.

Then we have the “events.”

Remember when a Dota event actually felt like an event?

Now it feels more like Valve remembered Dota exists during their lunch break and said:

“Uh… give them some cosmetics or something.”

The International used to feel like the World Cup of esports. The prize pool was legendary, Battle Pass season was exciting, everyone talked about TI, and even people who weren’t playing regularly came back to the game.

Now?

What’s the prize pool going to be? Who knows.

Are the rewards exciting? Not really.

Does Valve seem excited about TI anymore? Apparently not.

But hey, at least we can all be excited about whatever other project Valve is currently more interested in.

At this point, Dota 2 doesn’t feel like a game Valve is actively trying to grow.

It feels like an old pet they occasionally remember to feed.

The funniest part is that Dota 2 is still an incredible game underneath all of this. The gameplay, complexity, strategy, heroes, and competitive depth are things very few games can match.

And somehow, Valve’s greatest achievement is making people who love Dota recommend that other people never start playing it.

That takes talent.

So from someone who has wasted — sorry, invested — thousands of hours into Dota 2:

Do yourself a favor.

Play another MOBA.

Play League.

Play ROV.

Play something where you can at least pretend the developers want new players to stay.

Because judging by the smurf situation, matchmaking decisions, underwhelming events, shrinking excitement around The International, and Valve’s overall enthusiasm toward Dota…

I’m starting to think Valve isn’t trying to save Dota 2 anymore.

They’re just waiting to see how long it takes to die on its own.

And knowing Valve, when that finally happens, we’ll probably get a blog post six months later saying:

“Thanks for playing.”

review:
After surviving in lane since the earliest days of Dota All-Stars, I can personally attest to the extreme struggle and hardship of learning the intricacies of this game down to the most grueling and insignificant details.

If, despite the admonitions of other reviews or the warnings of your family and friends, you have still elected to proceed with this commitment to defend the Ancient, I implore you to weigh this short, solemn adjuration in advance. I believe the real truth is that concealed beneath the facade of entertainment, graphics, and gameplay lies the unperceived—and often perilous—illumination of critical life lessons.

During your pursuits, you will experience equally unavoidable resistance from adversaries and allies alike in the form of unbridled mental suffering, childish derision, and violent ridicule. This will occur despite your most sincere attempts to maintain amicable collaboration. You will be required by others to delve deep within your heart and soul to personally bear accountability for even the slightest perceived flaws or indiscretions. There will be no amelioration from this vitriolic, sacrificial behavior of the masses; you must aspire to defy one and all in order to advance your knowledge and skill set.

Once you embark on this journey, there will be moments of despair and resignation in which your mind will begin to abandon all hope—where personal improvement appears inconceivable. In these moments, you must battle yourself to find the strength to withstand the constant pressure of adversity and mend the fractures of intellectual stultification to discover your path to growth.

For those who persist and remain stoic, these transient and recurring feelings of dejection and pessimism are succeeded by some of the greatest thrills and emotions one can experience. As with almost everything in life, your experience throughout your matches within Dota will be a reflection of the resolve you've established as you lift the threshold of your skill level through dedication, time, and mental investment. The accomplishments chiseled out of hard work among your loyal and trusted companions will form an eternal bond which will always be remembered.

If you succeed in mastering the art of leading the Dire or Radiant to victory in this game, I truly believe there are no tasks in life too difficult for you to achieve.

I am a ranked-only player and its so frustrating that there are so many games (even like 4 out of 5 ) where you know you have lost during the picking phase or the first 10 minutes and you cant do anything about it. No matter how well you play, no matter how much you communicate, the game is lost and so is your rank.

The ranked system is a topic on its own. Unless you are a PRO in the Immortal rank, you have to play games while queuing for all the roles to gain tokens which you can use to play a game as the role you wanna play. Another thing is that you need so so many WINS to rank up. This combined with the ranking role queue system and toxic griefers I mentioned before means, that you wont get out of the rank for so long (Im still herald / guardian balancing around 900 MMR after 900+ hours).

I am kinda dissapointed that even tho I pay for Dota+ which gives you prediction of the quality of the match, it often doesnt even matter, because even with green communication and skill range you are not secured to have fun nor a chance to win. On the other hand, this game is just awesome mechanically and graphically. You will always have something to learn even after hundrets of hours. I haven't played that much...

But I'll write in hopes my review helps someone, somewhere make an informed decision.

This game will introduce you to the most toxic folks imaginable, worse then most customer service jobs provide. You'll be insulted in languages you don't understand and screamed at for god knows what, more often that any of us would like. That doesn't change once you escape lower brackets. 

This game will give you more sleepless nights than most addictions. You'll not want to end on a loss, so it's "just one more". You'll have a friend hop on when you're about to hop off, and it's "just one more". and eventually you'll find that this games activated something inside your brain, a switch you can't flip off. An itch that will never, ever feel successfully itched.

You'll never be good- or good enough. Right up to professional scene, you'll watch heralds and pro's alike misjudge and die to a neutral creep.. You'll cancel teleports and spells you didn't mean to. You'll miss last hits, and deny and ally that was going to survive.
But those moments that work ♥
You'll have incredible moments that leave you breathless, wondering how you pulled off that juke around the tree, into an incredible teleport escape- or that ultra kill that makes you want to jump out of your chair and cheer with your teammates.
Every game a unique experience with unexpected variables. No one single decision making or breaking a game, but hundreds of exciting smaller choices leading to thrilling conclusions- not always in your favor.

It's got the potential to ruin more friendships than monopoly, and take over your life..

But i guess it's a pretty cool game.

review:
WTF happened to this game?

I used to genuinely love Dota 2. I'd easily give it an 8/10. Now? It's honestly a 1/10, and it's not because of the gameplay—it's because of the absolute joke of a punishment system.

Imagine playing your heart out. You win your lane, rotate, help teammates, make the right calls, play objectives, end the game with the best stats on your team, and actually try to win. Then you get queued with a toxic 4-stack who spend the entire game flaming, griefing, and refusing to listen.

Guess what happens?

They all report you.

They can scream into voice chat, insult everyone, intentionally throw the game, and somehow they're perfectly fine because they're queued together. Meanwhile, the solo player who actually tried to win gets muted because the system blindly trusts mass reports.

How the hell does that make any sense?

Once you're muted, you can't even communicate objectives properly anymore. No shot calling. No warning teammates. No coordinating Roshan, smoke, or pushes. Congratulations—you've punished the player who's actually trying to win.

Valve seriously needs to stop relying on this lazy auto-report garbage. Do some actual analysis before punishing people. Look at the replay. Look at the chat logs. Look at player behavior. Look at who was griefing and who was actually playing the damn game.

Instead, the system is basically:
"Got reported enough? Cool, here's your punishment."

review:
I started playing Dota 2 thinking it was just another game. I was wrong.

This game taught me that winning isn't just about mechanics or having the strongest hero. It's about patience, teamwork, adapting to mistakes, and never giving up even when the game feels impossible.

I've celebrated incredible comebacks with complete strangers, and I've also experienced heartbreaking losses that stayed with me long after the match ended. Somehow, I always found myself clicking "Play Again."

Dota 2 isn't perfect. It can be frustrating, stressful, and sometimes toxic. But despite all of that, every match tells a different story. No two games ever feel exactly the same, and that's what keeps me coming back.

Over the years, Dota 2 has given me more than entertainment. It gave me unforgettable memories, friendships, and lessons about staying calm under pressure and learning from failure. It reminded me that even when you're behind, one good decision can change everything.

Whether you play for fun, to compete, or simply to spend time with friends, Dota 2 has a way of creating moments you'll remember for years.

Some games are just games.

Dota 2 became a part of my life.

review:
Dota 2 Review — 4,000 hours — Recommended (I guess)

4,000 hours. Let me repeat that. FOUR THOUSAND HOURS. That's 166 days of my life. I could have learned the violin, built a house, or watched my hair grow. Instead, I pulled it out.

I used to be competitive. Very competitive. I screamed at my teammates so much my neighbors thought I was being robbed every night at 11 PM. I lost faith in humanity around hour 800. By hour 2,000, I was convinced my teammates were losing on purpose ,a secret organization of psychos assigned specifically to MY team, every game, just to make me mad. Valve knows what I'm talking about. The matchmaking algorithm has a folder with my name on it.

i m 50 years old now
But here's the thing: I changed. I found peace. I don't scream anymore. I don't play carry anymore. I play support now, and I have discovered the true meaning of Dota:

I feed the enemy carry all game long.

And you know what? He's having a GREAT time. Best game of his life. Rampage at minute 20. Somewhere out there, a 14-year-old is smiling because of me.

After 4,000 hours, I finally learned the most important lesson this game can teach: you can't make your team happy. But you CAN make someone happy.

10/10. Would lose faith in humanity again.

As a result, I couldn't queue for ranked matches for a period of time, and it negatively affected my MMR and communication score, which significantly impacted my overall gaming experience.

The most frustrating part is that there is no support channel, dispute process, or appeal system where players can explain or contest these penalties. I understand the need to discourage intentional abandoning, but there should be a way to distinguish genuine technical issues from players who deliberately leave matches.

review:
Dota 2 is hands down the best MOBA on the market and for a while I shared the sentiment that it was the best game ever made. Gabe Newell plays it everyday and I think that it also is the best Valve game they have made. It got me interested in other MOBAs and liking the genre as a whole but in terms of execution, character viability, and existence of comeback mechanics, it by far makes this one the most rewarding to sink time into to get better. 
The game constantly evolves and while many people argue that it is more complicated now, in actuality the game is easier than when it released in 2012. I started playing in 2013 followed by a 4 year hiatus some time in between, picked up the game again and focusing on ranking up for the first time.
     Addressing the fact that the game is hard to understand is a natural part of the game. I have coached a few friends over the past 5 years and explained that it is okay for the game to not make sense. Similarly to playing chess it would be acceptable to not know what the pieces do and until you figure it out can you start to engage with the game and make sense of what to do and how to do it. You do not need to have a PHD to be able to play this game or find some enjoyment. I have found many people that can barely tie their own shoes and they manage just fine.
Toxicity is not unique to this game but it does give you tools to be creative with it. Think of counter strike where the presence of toxicity is one thing but then you can blind with a flashbang, team kill, and so on and so forth. I still think hands down Dead By daylight is the most toxic game by far if I were to be completely honest based on my experience.
    The character design has the same flare that other valve games are known for so if the game is too competitive then there are player made games similar to what you'd find in Roblox or Garry's mod in the games "Arcade" which was one of the ways I eased a friends into playing the base game. The cosmetics are divided into components so you can mix and match allowing this feature to make the game into a dress up sim. 
In conclusion I do think everyone could find some degree of enjoyment in this type of game so long as there is an interest in wanting to both learn and improve.

review:
I've been playing this game since its earliest days. The first five years were incredible, but every attempt I've made to come back since has been nothing but disappointment.

It pains me to say this because I used to be a huge fan, but with every update, Dota 2 feels less like Dota and more like League of Legends. The identity that made this game legendary has been stripped away in favor of chasing trends and selling cosmetics. New skins are uninspired garbage, while many of the classic ones that players actually loved have been removed.

Every new "feature" or "mechanic" seems designed to bloat the game rather than improve it. System requirements keep climbing for no good reason, yet performance somehow keeps getting worse. Even on a modern PC, the game stutters, lags, and the servers frequently fail to respond. It's honestly embarrassing for a game that's been around this long.

After thousands of hours invested, I've finally had enough. I'm going back to Dota 1—the original game that actually respected its own identity. Dota 2 stopped being a true successor years ago. It abandoned the formula that made it great in favor of squeezing more money out of its player base. It's no longer the game I fell in love with, and that's the biggest disappointment of all.

I've played DotA since over 20 years ago.  This iteration has smooth graphics and everything and the game is great...  that's not the problem.

How is there not a surrender option in this game?  For a game that by definition takes a LONG time to play a match, it's a little obnoxious to have to play a clearly losing game for 30-60 minutes just not to get punished.  I am adult with things to do, I am not investing my time in sitting around and pretending to play just to placate your crappy system.  And when you do get punished?  You have to win two single draft games to get out of time-out.  The problem is that no one is playing that you sit in matchmaking for 10 minutes before giving up and realizing this game has a SERIOUS systemic blind spot. 

I'd argue it was better when people just left and that was that - the remaining players scaled quicker as a result and created a different strategic situation when that happened.  I get serious punishments for ranked play, but for casual unranked?  Be real.  This is a game, not my job.

Way to ruin a classic.

review:
[h2]The Undisputed King of Competitive Gaming[/h2]
Having walked the long road from the original WC3 DotA, through the early days of Dota 2 and the Reborn update, right up to the current patch, I can state this with absolute certainty: Dota 2 was, is, and likely always will be one of the most intense and deeply rewarding competitive games ever created.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3763540634
[h2]The Duality of the Community[/h2]
There is almost [b]no in-between.[/b]

The matchmaking experience here is a perfect, [b]chaotic 50/50 split.[/b] Every match is a literal coin toss. You will either get a whiny man-child who didn't get his mid lane, instantly destroys his items at minute zero, and marches down the lane to feed — or you will be blessed with an incredibly competent, understanding team that knows exactly how to play the game (ideally, in absolute, telepathic silence).

[h2]True Free-to-Play[/h2]
Unlike many modern titles, the monetization here is genuinely optional. The game constantly showers you with bonuses and drops. You can play completely free of charge without spending a single dime, and you will still watch your inventory naturally fill up with sweet cosmetic sets and skins.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3764613733
[h2]The Arcade Universe[/h2]
It's literally a whole [b]different game within a game.[/b]

The Arcade section isn't just a feature; it's a thriving multiverse of its own. This is the legendary breeding ground for massive hits like Auto Chess and Custom Hero Clash, drawing [b]tens of thousands of concurrent players[/b] just to have fun.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3764780833
[h2]Justice Finally Served[/h2]
And the absolute [b]cherry on top?[/b] Surprisingly, the report system actually works now. Toxic behavior genuinely gets punished, making the MMR grind far more bearable.

review:
I've played League for 12+ years. I really like Dota 2 a lot. The micro seems less difficult than in League, but the cheese feels more extreme. I find myself focusing much more on macro play in Dota. In League, it's more about every tiny step—dodging skillshots, landing your own, and winning extended fights through constant maneuvering and looking for small windows of opportunity.

With Dota, it feels more based around powerful point-and-click abilities and very over-the-top, often unavoidable hero powers. The game is often about setting up numerical advantages and catching people off guard with smoke. Both are fun in their own ways. I love all the active items in Dota and their relatively short cooldowns. It's a very fun game. I also really like how massive the jungle is—even as a support in very drawn-out games, I can end up with 300+ CS.

I'd highly recommend this game to people coming from League. It might just refresh your love for MOBAs.

review:
There’s a certain sentiment that games like League or Dota are an addiction, something that players can’t unlatch themselves from; the uninstall button evading every impulse, as the blood and sanity is sapped year after year. Endless reviews of people thousands of hours into the void, telling, warning people of its pull. 
I can’t agree with them. This game is even richer and more rewarding than when I started 11 years ago. While life drains every joy around me, Dota is the constant that provides endless engagement. 

The game is ever-changing. I can’t think of any other online experience that switches up the meta so frequently, and yet it rarely ever feels unbalanced or broken. This malleable game space is the reason nobody is clamouring for a Dota 3 — we’ve passed that point 8 mega-patches ago. Production value is consistent with Valve’s other games: polished to an unbelievable degree; impeccable sound design, you can close your eyes and still know what’s going on; slick Source 2 visuals; intuitive gameplay, options for options, play how you want. 

I think it helps a lot if you treat it entirely as a sport; framing something like this as a game implies victory at the end of the tunnel — credits, achievements, fulfilment. Not so. The only end is artificial, a truncation on the user’s end, be it shifting priorities, loss of interest, or death. You will lose. A lot. People that don’t realise this are only satisfied with those precious victories; maybe winning half the time is why so much resentment is visible online. Once you do reframe it, you’re free. 
Free to make friends as I have. Free to try new builds, new mind games, new team comps. 
Drag people through your off-lane Pugna arc. Bait enemies with your team, pull off the sickest 4 man black hole, get it cancelled by a rogue stun not meant for you. Blink into the enemy-infested fog and hook your reluctant teammate in. 

Engage with its complexities; this isn’t the sport for champions. Prepare to not just die, but lose. Every low met with a high, every report met with a commend, or a memory, or a friend, or just the buzz you need when everything around you persists at knocking you down. 
Lock in. Pump those hours, every one a notch of perseverance. Wave after wave, blood and adrenaline rising. Ten people in a gauntlet for courage, boldness and survival, each doing the only thing they can: their best. This is the sport for heroes.

review:
The matchmaking system really sucks when team members have very different ranks.

The game is also overfilled with bots, smurfs, scripters, and sometimes even cheaters using map hacks.

When you play solo, the game is actually very good and the matchmaking usually feels fair. The problem starts when you play in a party of 2–5 people with different ranks.

We constantly end up against bot lobbies used to derank smurf accounts, or smurf lobbies full of unranked or lowest-rank players who somehow play like gods and barely make any mistakes.

If our party does not fill the whole team, the matchmaking often fills the remaining slots on our side with complete beginners or very weak players. That completely destroys any meaningful teamplay and makes the skill imbalance even worse.

Otherwise, this is a very good game, but this matchmaking issue makes it simply not worth my time.

Ranks and matchmaking need to be based on actual player skill. The system should also be able to identify and filter out deliberately lost matches that clearly do not represent a player’s real or peak performance.
